THEORY.title: About these notes
THEORY.html:
Scope: Week 1 (HTML, JavaScript recap, web services and APIs), Week 2 (CSS), Week 3 (Bootstrap), Weeks 4 to 6 (Vue fundamentals, events, computed, lists, async/Axios, components), the Week 5/6 Node/Express/MongoDB backend, and the lab-test material for the four exam topics (worked solutions, troubleshooting, exam rules, quick-reference lookups, self-check with answers).

Detected module type: Programming / CS (front-end web development). "Worked example" here means annotated code plus the result you should see. "Gotcha" means a syntax or ordering trap. Visuals are flowcharts, sequence diagrams and decision trees.

Exam format: the archive contains two lab tests (2026 TRIAL and 2024). Both are open-book, 2-hour, code-it-yourself lab tests with four questions in this order: Q1 CSS, Q2 Bootstrap, Q3 Basic Vue, Q4 Vue + Axios. That is exactly your four cheat-sheet topics, so the self-check section (§15) mimics that format.

Source tags: [Wk2 slides] means lecture slides, [wk2example5.html] means an example file, [CSS Quiz p3] means a page of CSS Quiz.pdf, [LT26 q3.vue] means the 2026 trial lab test resources, [LT24 q4.vue] means the 2024 Practice Lab. (added context) marks anything not in your materials that I added so the syntax makes sense. Worked solutions to lab-test questions are my own unless a solution file is named.

Gaps in the course materials (read this first)

  • Screenshots are not extractable. Slides say "Browser Preview" but the pictures carry no text. I derived expected results from the matching .html/.vue example files, which I read line by line. I did not run the code in a browser, so all traces are done by reading only.
  • Linked videos and websites (inline vs block, relative vs absolute, box-sizing videos; w3schools; getbootstrap.com) were not provided. I did not invent their contents.
  • Lab-test figures: the question papers show target screenshots that I can only partly read. Where a requirement depends on a picture I say so and base the answer on the written text.
  • Sample solutions for the Extra Exercise PDFs (Vue Basics, Vue Components, Vue State Management) are not in the archive, only the question PDFs. I used them for syntax hints (for example maxlength binding, toFixed, toLocaleString), not as answer keys.
  • Only skimmed in the lab-test material: Week 1 (HTML/JS recap), the JSBasics, JSDom and JSAJAX extras, the Express/MongoDB server code and the .pptx MongoDB guide are not part of the four lab-test topics. They are covered from the course notes in chapters 2 to 4 and 9 to 11. Pinia is covered only by a short optional appendix (chapter 16).
  • Not usable: node_modules/ folders in the zip are empty link stubs. rh.chan.2025.zip (nested) is a near-copy of the 2026 trial folder; only q3.vue differs (it lacks :key="log.id").
  • Archive files that look like partial student answers: LT26 q1.css (border: 2px is incomplete), LT26 q3.vue (stock shown without brackets), LT26 q2.vue (already fixed). I treat them as evidence, not as model answers.

THEORY.title: Big-Picture Overview and Exam Format
THEORY.subtitle: Chapter overview
THEORY.html:
The course stacks four tools. Each one only makes sense once you know the one before it.

  • HTML is the content (nouns), CSS is the presentation (adjectives), JS is the behaviour (verbs) [Wk2 slides, "What is CSS?"].
  • Vanilla CSS styles elements with your own rules.
  • Bootstrap is a big pre-written CSS + JS file (bootstrap.min.css + bootstrap.min.js) [Wk3 slides]. You style by adding class names instead of writing rules.
  • Vue removes manual DOM work: you declare how the UI looks for a given state and Vue updates the DOM [Wk4 slides, "What is a Reactive Application?"].
  • Axios is the library Vue apps use to talk to a server asynchronously [Wk5 slides].

Diagram: how the four topics layer (inferred from the Wk2 to Wk6 progression).

HTML: structure→Vanilla CSS: your own rules→Bootstrap 5.3: ready-made classes + JS
HTML: structure→Vue 3 SFC: template + script + style→Axios: async HTTP→REST server: Express + JSON
Bootstrapclass names in template →Vue
Vanilla CSSstyle scoped / import css →Vue

Read it left to right: CSS and Bootstrap are two ways to style; Vue is where the HTML lives in Weeks 4 to 6 (inside .vue files); Axios is how a Vue component gets or changes server data. Dotted lines mean "used inside".

Diagram: what the lab test asks, with marks (2026 TRIAL total 25; 2024 total 25).

Q1 Vanilla CSS
  • 2026: 5 marks, 2024: 9 marks
  • centre text, radius, hover, cursor
  • selectors and specificity
  • flex and grid
Q2 Bootstrap
  • 2026: 5 marks, 2024: 5 marks
  • navbar-expand-md
  • col and row-cols with breakpoints
  • badges and utility classes
Q3 Basic Vue
  • 2026: 5 marks, 2024: 6 marks
  • v-for, v-if / v-else, :disabled
  • v-model, click handlers
  • setTimeout and array methods
Q4 Vue and Axios
  • 2026: 10 marks, 2024: 5 marks
  • GET on mount
  • POST and DELETE
  • class binding for Yes / No

Notice that Q4 is worth the most in 2026 (10 of 25). Every Axios question follows the same shape: load on mount, add via POST, delete via DELETE, then show the result with v-for. The Vue + Axios chapter (§8) is built around that shape.

How to use this file. Each section starts with what it is and when to use it, then the syntax, then a gotcha box. Worked lab-test answers are in §9. If you are stuck mid-exam, jump to §14.

THEORY.title: The full stack, from HTML to database
THEORY.html:
This course builds a full web application stack, one layer at a time:

HTML (content, "nouns")  →  CSS (presentation, "adjectives")  →  JavaScript (behaviour, "verbs")
        ↓
Bootstrap (pre-built CSS/JS components so you don't hand-roll every button/grid)
        ↓
Vue.js (a JavaScript framework that makes the page reactive: data changes → UI updates automatically,
        instead of you manually calling document.getElementById(...).innerText = ... everywhere)
        ↓
Axios (lets your Vue frontend talk to a backend over HTTP — asynchronously, without freezing the page)
        ↓
Node.js + Express.js + (file storage OR MongoDB via Mongoose) — the backend that stores and serves data

Each week adds one layer without discarding the previous ones — by Week 5 you have a Vue frontend (styled with Bootstrap) making Axios calls to an Express backend that persists blog posts either to a JSON file or to a MongoDB Atlas cluster.

The running example used from Week 1 through Week 5 is progressively the same idea: a Blog Service with posts that have a subject/title, an entry/content, and a mood. It starts as static HTML, then gets styled, then becomes a Vue table, then gets full CRUD (Create/Read/Update/Delete) wired to a real backend.

THEORY.title: What HTML Is
THEORY.html:
HTML (HyperText Markup Language) is a tree of tags/elements. Tags can carry attributes, and attributes carry values:

<!doctype html>
<html>
  <head>
    <title>Hello World</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <p style="text-align:right">This is a paragraph.</p>
  </body>
</html>

Every HTML document can be thought of as a DOM (Document Object Model) tree — building or modifying a page is really growing/trimming that tree. This mental model matters later: Vue's reactivity and vanilla JS's document.getElementById(...) are both just different ways of touching this same tree.

THEORY.title: Core Tag Reference
THEORY.html:
Tag Example Purpose
Header <h1>...</h1> … <h6> Section headings, in decreasing importance
Paragraph <p>...</p> Block of text
Image <img src="..."> Embed an image (self-closing, no closing tag needed)
Table <table><tr><td>...</td></tr></table> Tabular data (tr = row, td = cell, th = header cell)
Input <input type="text"> A form field; behaviour depends entirely on type
Button <button type="submit">Submit</button> Clickable control
Dropdown <select><option>...</option></select> Choice list
Ordered list <ol><li>...</li></ol> Numbered list
Unordered list <ul><li>...</li></ul> Bulleted list
Anchor <a href="abc.site">My Homepage</a> Hyperlink
Form <form action="newpage.html" method="GET">...</form> Wraps inputs; method is GET (data in URL) or POST (data in body)
Frame <iframe width="560" height="315" src="..."> Embeds another page/video inline

Styling-related (structural, not visual by themselves):

Tag Use
<div id="div1">...</div> Generic block-level container — the standard hook for CSS/JS targeting
<span class="fav">...</span> Generic inline container — like div but doesn't force a line break
<nav>...</nav> Semantically marks navigation links

HTML5 semantic tags (these exist so both browsers and other developers/screen readers understand the page's structure, not just its visual layout):

Tag Meaning
<header>...</header> Introductory content for a page or section
<footer>...</footer> Footer info: copyright, related links
<section>...</section> A thematic grouping of content
<article>...</article> A standalone, self-contained piece of content (blog post, news article)
<aside>...</aside> Secondary/tangential content (sidebar)

💡 Why semantic tags matter beyond looking "correct": a <div> and a <section> can look pixel-identical, but only one tells a screen reader (or a search engine) "this is a distinct thematic block." Bootstrap's ARIA discussion in Week 3 builds directly on this idea.

THEORY.title: Input Types & Attributes
THEORY.html:
Modern HTML gives you many specialised <input> types instead of validating everything yourself in JavaScript:

type= value Behaviour
color Opens a color picker
date Opens a date picker
email Checks for a well-formed email (must contain @)
file File-select field with a "Browse" button
number Accepts only numeric values (can pair with min/max)
range Slider control
search, tel, time, url Specialised keyboards/validation on mobile, semantic hinting on desktop

Common attributes that constrain those inputs:

Attribute Effect
max / min Bounds for numeric-ish inputs
maxlength Max character count
readonly Field shows a value but can't be edited
required Field cannot be submitted empty
selected Marks a <option> as the default choice in a <select>
checked Marks a checkbox/radio as pre-selected

Worked example — default <select> option (from wk1ex1):

<select>
    <option value='Monday'>Monday</option>
    <option value='Tuesday'>Tuesday</option>
    <option value='Sunday' selected>Sunday</option>   <!-- 'selected' makes this the default, regardless of list order -->
</select>

The selected attribute — not the option's position in the list — determines the default. This is a common early misconception: reordering <option>s does not change the default; you must move (or add) selected.

THEORY.title: Meta Tags
THEORY.html:
<meta> tags carry metadata — information about the page that isn't rendered but is read by browsers/search engines:

<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <meta name="description" content="Free Web tutorials">
  <meta name="keywords" content="HTML,CSS,XML,JavaScript">
  <meta name="author" content="John Doe">
  <!-- Controls how the page scales on mobile devices -->
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
</head>

The viewport meta tag is the one you'll use in every single project — without it, mobile browsers render the page at desktop width and then zoom out, defeating any responsive CSS/Bootstrap you write.

THEORY.title: JavaScript in the Browser — Recap (Week 1)
THEORY.subtitle: Chapter overview
THEORY.html: This is positioned as a recap from a prior course (WAD1/IS113), so it moves quickly through fundamentals before Vue replaces most of this manual DOM work from Week 4 onward.

THEORY.title: Naming Conventions
THEORY.html:
Style Example Typical use in JS
snake_case (underscore) first_name, master_card Rare in JS; common in Python/Ruby
UpperCamelCase (PascalCase) FirstName, MasterCard Class names, Vue component names
lowerCamelCase firstName, masterCard Standard for JS variables/functions

THEORY.title: Script Placement
THEORY.html:
<html>
 <head>
   <script>/* runs before page is rendered — use only if you must run before render */</script>
 </head>
 <body>
   ...
   <script>/* most common placement: end of <body>, so the DOM exists before your script touches it */</script>
 </body>
</html>

Rule of thumb: put <script> at the bottom of <body> unless the script must run before anything renders.

THEORY.title: Event Handling (Vanilla JS)
THEORY.html:
<p id="time"></p>
<button onclick="document.getElementById('time').innerText = Date()">What time is it?</button>
  • document.getElementById(id) retrieves the DOM element with that id.
  • .innerText is the visible text content of an element — assigning to it overwrites what's shown.
Event Fires when...
onclick user clicks the element
onchange element's value has changed (fires on blur/commit)
oninput user types/inputs (fires on every keystroke)
onmouseover / onmouseout mouse enters/leaves the element
onkeypress a key is pressed
onload the browser finishes loading the page

💡 onchange vs oninput: oninput fires continuously as the user types (good for live character counters); onchange only fires once the user leaves the field (good for expensive validation you don't want running on every keystroke). This distinction resurfaces in Vue's v-model — Vue's default v-model on text inputs behaves like oninput (updates on every keystroke).

THEORY.title: Promises, Async/Await (Recap)
THEORY.html:
A Promise represents the eventual result of an asynchronous operation. It has three states:

State Meaning
Pending operation still running
Fulfilled operation succeeded → the code after await keeps running
Rejected operation failed → the catch block runs 
// fetch() returns a Promise immediately; the request runs in the background.
// async/await lets you write the code so it reads top-to-bottom like synchronous code.
async function getPost(id) {
  try {
    const response = await fetch(`https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts/${id}`)
    const data = await response.json()
    console.log(data)
  } catch (error) {
    console.error(error)
  }
}

await can only be used inside a function declared async. It pauses that function (not the whole program) until the awaited Promise settles.

Worked example — GET and POST with fetch() (from wk1ex4):

async function getPost(){
    const id = document.getElementById("postID").value;
    const response = await fetch(`https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts/${id}`);
    const data = await response.json();
    document.getElementById("getResult").textContent = JSON.stringify(data, null, 4);
}

async function createPost(){
    const title = document.getElementById("title").value;
    const body  = document.getElementById("body").value;
    const response = await fetch("https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts", {
        method: "POST",
        headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
        body: JSON.stringify({ title: title, body: body, userId: 1 })
    });
    const data = await response.json();
    document.getElementById("postResult").textContent = JSON.stringify(data, null, 4);
}

Note the three things every POST needs: (1) method: "POST", (2) a Content-Type header telling the server the body is JSON, (3) a body that is a string (JSON.stringify(...)) — you cannot pass a raw JS object as the body.

THEORY.title: Web Services & APIs (Week 1)
THEORY.subtitle: Chapter overview
THEORY.html:
• A Web API is a reusable, well-packaged set of functionality exposed over the web (e.g. Google Maps' API lets you embed maps without writing your own mapping engine).
  • API keys identify and authenticate the caller so the API isn't misused. Treat them as secrets — never hard-code them in a public/committed file (see the dotenv/config.env discussion in §10.5, which exists precisely to solve this problem).

Example: OpenWeatherMap

https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather?q=London,uk&APPID=yourapikey

Example: JSONPlaceholder (no key needed — good for practicing without setup):

GET  https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts/1
POST https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts

Take-away: HTML = content; CSS = style; JS = dynamic behaviour; Web APIs = "online libraries" your JS/Vue code can call.

THEORY.title: Vanilla CSS (Week 2)
THEORY.subtitle: Chapter overview
THEORY.html: CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) separates what the page says from how it looks. It makes pages look consistent site-wide and lets you change a whole site by editing one file [Wk2 slides, "What is CSS?"].

THEORY.title: Three ways to attach CSS
THEORY.html:
Method Where the code goes Scope Use when Priority
Inline style="..." attribute on one tag in <body> That one tag Quick one-off override; use sparingly Highest
Internal <style> block inside <head> Whole page Single-page project Same as external; last defined wins
External Separate .css file linked with <link> Every page that links it Multi-page sites (best practice) Same as internal; last defined wins

[Wk2 slides, "Using CSS" tables]

<!-- 1. INLINE [wk2example2.html]: semicolon between declarations -->
<h2 style="color:red;">CAUTION: Icy Road Conditions</h2>

<!-- 2. INTERNAL [wk2example3.html] -->
<head>
  <style>
    h2 { color: green; }
  </style>
</head>

<!-- 3. EXTERNAL [wk2ex4pg1.html]: link goes in <head>; href is the path to the .css file -->
<head>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="wk2ex4.css">
</head>

Order matters between internal and external. If both set h2 { color }, whichever appears later in the <head> wins [wk2example7.html]. Put your <link> first and your <style> after it if you want the internal block to override.

In Vue you use the same idea: <style scoped> inside a .vue file is "internal but only for this component", and import './q1.css' inside <script setup> pulls in an external file [LT26 q1.vue]. See §7.3.

THEORY.title: Rule syntax
THEORY.html:
/* selector { property: value; } */
p { color: red; }

/* several declarations: each ends with a semicolon */
p {
  color: red;
  font-style: italic;
  text-align: center;
}

/* group selectors: same rule for several elements */
h1, h2 { color: blue; }

Most common CSS mistake: forgetting the semicolon after a declaration [Wk2 slides, "CSS Syntax"]. The next property is silently ignored. Comments are /* ... */ (not //).

THEORY.title: Selectors: what am I targeting?
THEORY.html:
Selector Syntax Matches Example from the source
Element p every <p> p { color: blue; } [wk2example4.html]
Class .normal every element with class="normal" (many allowed) .normal { color: black; } [wk2example5.html]
ID #emphasis the one element with id="emphasis" #emphasis { font-style: italic; }
Universal * everything * { box-sizing: border-box; } [LT26 q4_readonly.css]
Grouping h1, h2 each listed selector table, th, td { border: 1px solid black; }
Compound (no space) day.today element and class together day.today {...} [LT26 q1.css]
Descendant (space) .rating ul li li anywhere inside ul inside .rating .rating ul li {...} [LT24 q1.css]
Attribute input[type=text] inputs whose type is text [wk2example20.html]
Pseudo-class tr:hover element in a state tr:hover {...} [wk2example16.html]
Nth child tr:nth-child(odd) odd rows (even also works) [wk2example16.html]
Checked input:checked ticked checkboxes/radios [Wk2 slides, "Exotic Examples"]
Negation :not(p) every element that is not a <p> [Wk2 slides]

Multiple classes on one element: <p class="normal center"> gets both .normal and .center rules [wk2example5.html].

The infographic in [CSS Quiz p3] also lists combinators (they add no specificity): descendant (space), child >, adjacent sibling +, general sibling ~.

Source issues to know about. - [wk2example4.html] uses id="emphasis" twice and asks "is it a problem?". Yes: IDs must be unique per page. Use a class for repeated styling. - The slide's "Exotic Examples" shows input:selected. That is not a CSS selector; the working one is input:checked (the description on the slide matches :checked).

THEORY.title: Specificity and the cascade: which rule wins?
THEORY.html:
When two rules set the same property on the same element, the browser picks one.

Step 1: specificity score (ID, Class, Element) from [CSS Quiz p3]:

Selector type Example Score (ID, Class, Element) Rank
Inline style="" <p style="..."> beats all selectors highest
ID #header (1, 0, 0) 1
Class / attribute / pseudo-class .btn, [type="text"], :hover, :first-child (0, 1, 0) 2
Element / pseudo-element p, div, ::before (0, 0, 1) 3
Universal * (0, 0, 0) 4 (weakest)
  • A declaration flag !important overrides selector scores; it is not part of a score [CSS Quiz p3].
  • Ties: the rule that appears later in the source wins [CSS Quiz p3, "Quick tip"].

Step 2: origin order [Wk2 slides, "CSS Cascading Order"]:

  1. Inline style (highest)
  2. Internal / external, same priority, last defined wins
  3. Browser default (lowest)

Diagram: decision flow for "which colour does my text get?"

StepQuestionIf yesIf no
1Is one of the rules an inline style attribute?Inline winsGo to step 2
2Do the rules have different specificity? (ID > class > element)Higher specificity winsGo to step 3
3Same specificityThe LATER rule in source order wins—

!important overrides all of the above.

Read top to bottom. Notice you almost never need !important; fixing the order or specificity is cleaner.

Worked trace [wk2example7.html] (by reading only). The page links wk2ex7.css (h3 blue, then h3 pink) and its own <style> (h2 grey, then h2 red). The <h2> has style="color: green; color: blue" style="color: yellow;".

Element Candidates Result Why
<h3> external: blue, then pink pink same priority, last wins
first <h2> grey, red, then inline blue inline beats stylesheets; with a repeated style attribute the first attribute applies [Wk2 slides, "CSS Conflict Resolving"], and inside it the last declaration (blue) wins
second <h2> grey, red red last defined wins

Class vs element: a class rule beats an element rule, even if the element rule is written later [wk2example5.html]. If your p { color: blue } "does not work" on <p class="normal">, the class rule is winning.

THEORY.title: The box model
THEORY.html:
Every element is a box: content (text/images), then padding (space between content and border, inside), then border (visible line), then margin (space outside the border). Padding and margin are transparent [Wk2 slides, "The Box Model"]. Inner to outer: content, padding, border, margin [CSS Quiz Q5].

.box {
  width: 50px;  height: 50px;
  padding: 10px;                       /* inside the border */
  border: 2px solid red;               /* width style colour */
  border-radius: 10%;                  /* rounded corners; 50% on a square makes a circle */
  margin: 30px 50px 30px 50px;         /* outside the border */
}

Shorthand for margin and padding [wk2example14.html comments]:

Values given Meaning
margin: 30px all four sides
margin: 30px 50px top+bottom = 30px, left+right = 50px
margin: 30px 50px 10px top = 30, left+right = 50, bottom = 10
margin: 30px 50px 30px 50px top, right, bottom, left (clockwise)

Single sides: margin-top/right/bottom/left, padding-top/..., border-left, border-top and so on (for example border-left: 5px dotted red) [wk2example13.html]. Margin values can be auto, a length, a % of the containing element's width, or inherit [Wk2 slides].

Centring a block horizontally: give it a width and margin: auto [wk2example12.html].

.centerdiv1 { width: 800px;     margin: auto; }   /* fixed: scrolls sideways on small screens */
.centerdiv2 { max-width: 800px; margin: auto; }   /* shrinks when the window is smaller: prefer this */
.childsquare { width: 50%; }                      /* % is relative to the PARENT's width */

box-sizing [Wk2 slides, "Box-sizing"; CSS Quiz Q2, p5, p6]:

content-box (default) border-box (recommended)
width covers content only content + padding + border
Total size width + padding + border exactly width
Example (width:200px; padding:20px; border:5px) renders 250px renders 200px (content shrinks to 150px) 
* { box-sizing: border-box; }   /* put this at the top of your stylesheet */

Exam use: if a form input with width:100% overflows its container, add box-sizing: border-box [wk2example20.html].

Box-sizing in frameworks

Set * { box-sizing: border-box; } globally near the top of your stylesheet. It makes layout maths dramatically more predictable, and it is what virtually every modern CSS framework (Bootstrap included) does by default.

THEORY.title: Units and colours
THEORY.html:
Kind Units Notes
Absolute px (1px = 1/96 inch), in, cm px is what you use most
Relative % (of parent), em (of parent's font-size), vw (1% of viewport width) [Wk2 slides]
Also used in the files (added context) vh (1% of viewport height), rem, fr (grid only, §5.15) min-height: 90vh [wk2example23.html], 100vh [LT26 q1.css], 2rem [LT24 q2_readonly.css]

Colour formats [wk2example11.html]:

color: red;                       /* named: lavender, darkslateblue, royalblue, lightsteelblue, gold ... */
color: #eab01c;                   /* hex */
color: rgb(30, 200, 0);           /* red green blue, 0-255 */
color: rgba(13, 90, 140, 1);      /* a = alpha: 0 fully transparent, 1 fully opaque */
background-image: radial-gradient(circle, #051937, #002667, #112e98, #4a2ec4, #8712eb);  /* [wk2example10.html] */

THEORY.title: Text and font properties
THEORY.html:
Property Values seen Example [wk2example8.html]
color any colour color: whitesmoke;
text-align left, right, center text-align: right;
text-decoration line-through, underline, none text-decoration: line-through;
text-transform capitalize, uppercase text-transform: capitalize;
text-indent length text-indent: 50px;
font-family comma list, first available font is used 'Times New Roman', Times, serif
font-style italic font-style: italic;
font-size px, vw, % (default 16px) font-size: 3vw;
font-weight bold, numbers font-weight: bold;
background-color any colour background-color: bisque;

Source typos, do not copy: font-weight: semi-bold [wk2example23.html] is invalid (use 600); rgb(30,200,0,) [wk2example11.html] has a stray comma; padding: 10px, 10px [marketplace.html] should have no comma.

THEORY.title: display and hiding things
THEORY.html:
display says how an element sits relative to its neighbours [Wk2 slides, "Display properties"]:

Value Behaviour Typical use
block starts on a new line, takes the full width <div>, <p>, <h1> by default
inline flows next to the previous element; width/height are ignored <span>, <a> by default; [wk2example9.html] makes <p> inline
inline-block flows inline but accepts width/height/margins buttons in a row (added context: the slide only names it and links a video)
none element removed from view hide/show with JS (Vue prefers v-if, §7.7)
flex / grid turns the element into a layout container §5.14 and §5.15

Every HTML element has a default display. An unknown tag such as <day> in [LT26 q1.vue] is inline by default, which is why q1.css sets day { display: flex; ... } (added context).

THEORY.title: Backgrounds
THEORY.html:
background-color: lightblue;
background-image: url("./img/search.jpg");   /* [wk2example21.html] */
background-position: 5px;
background-repeat: no-repeat;
padding-left: 40px;                          /* leave room for the icon so text does not overlap */

THEORY.title: Positioning
THEORY.html:
position decides how an element is placed. Offsets (top, right, bottom, left) only do something when position is not static [Wk2 slides; CSS Quiz p10].

Value Positioned relative to Keeps its space in the flow? Use for
static (default) normal flow yes ordinary layout
relative its own normal position (left:20px nudges it right) yes (original space reserved) small nudges; also makes a parent for absolute children
absolute nearest positioned (non-static) ancestor no (removed from flow) badges, overlays, dropdown panels
fixed the browser window no pinned sidebars/menus that ignore scrolling
sticky scroll position: acts relative until the offset is reached, then sticks like fixed yes until stuck sticky headers 
.relative { position: relative; left: 30px; }                       /* [wk2example17.html] */
.absolute { position: absolute; top: 250px; right: 0; }             /* inside a relative parent */
.fixed    { position: fixed;    top: 0;     right: 0; }
.sticky   { position: sticky;   top: 0; }                           /* sticky needs an offset */
img       { position: absolute; left: 0; top: 0; z-index: -1; }     /* behind the text */

z-index sets stacking order for positioned elements; larger is in front, negative goes behind [Wk2 slides, "Overlapping Elements"]. Percentages for offsets use the containing block [CSS Quiz p10].

  • Absolute with no positioned parent places the element relative to the page, not the card you meant. Add position: relative to the intended parent.
  • sticky without top: 0 (or another offset) never sticks. z-index does nothing on position: static [CSS Quiz p10 "Common traps"].
  • A side menu "that does not scroll with the content" [Extra Exercises CSS Q1] is position: fixed on the nav, plus padding-left (or margin-left) on the main content equal to the menu width [fruit_alternative_solution.html].

float: left / float: right appears in the CSS practice solutions to place images beside text (added context). Bootstrap's float-start / float-end are the same idea (§6.3).

Relative vs absolute, and scroll behaviour

Value Affected by scroll?
static (default) Yes
relative Yes
absolute Yes (scrolls with the positioned ancestor it is placed against)
fixed No: stays in place relative to the viewport
sticky Partially: scrolls normally, then sticks once the scroll offset is reached (relative to the nearest scrolling ancestor)

The key distinction: surrounding elements do not know a relative element moved (its original space is still reserved). An absolute element is removed from the flow entirely, so its neighbours collapse into the space it would have occupied. This is the number-one cause of "why did my layout jump" bugs.

THEORY.title: Flexbox (one dimension)
THEORY.html:
What / when: lays items out along one axis (a row or a column). Use it for navbars, toolbars, button groups, card rows and centring [Wk2 slides "Flexbox vs Grid"].

.container {
  display: flex;                   /* turn on flexbox; direct children become flex items */
  flex-direction: row;             /* row (default), column, row-reverse, column-reverse */
  justify-content: space-between;  /* along the MAIN axis */
  align-items: center;             /* along the CROSS axis */
  gap: 16px;                       /* space between items */
  flex-wrap: wrap;                 /* allow items to wrap onto new lines */
}
.item { flex: 1; }                 /* takes an equal share of remaining space */
Property (on container) Values Meaning
flex-direction row, column, row-reverse, column-reverse sets the main axis
justify-content flex-start, center, flex-end, space-between, space-around (space-evenly also appears in the quiz infographic) distribution on the main axis
align-items flex-start, center, flex-end, stretch, baseline alignment on the cross axis
flex-wrap nowrap, wrap, wrap-reverse wrapping
gap length spacing between items

Item-level properties from the [CSS Quiz p15 infographic]: order, flex-grow (default 0), flex-shrink (default 1), flex-basis, and the shorthand flex: grow shrink basis (for example flex: 1 1 200px).

The axes swap when you change direction [CSS Quiz Q7, p15]. With flex-direction: row, justify-content is horizontal. With flex-direction: column, justify-content becomes vertical and align-items controls the horizontal alignment (the quiz's correct answer). Memorise: justify-content = main axis, align-items = cross axis, not "horizontal/vertical".

Centre text both ways inside a box (this is Q1 Part A of the 2026 trial [LT26 q1.css]):

day { display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center; }

More flexbox details

  • align-content aligns multiple lines along the cross axis. It only has an effect with flex-wrap: wrap and takes the same values as justify-content.
  • justify-content also accepts space-evenly (equal space between items and at both ends).
  • flex-wrap values: nowrap (default), wrap, wrap-reverse.
  • justify-content does not affect cross-axis alignment, and align-items does not create space between items (only the space-* values of justify-content do that).

THEORY.title: CSS Grid (two dimensions)
THEORY.html:
What / when: rows and columns at once. Use it for page skeletons, dashboards and galleries [Wk2 slides].

.grid-container {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 200px 1fr 200px;   /* fixed, flexible, fixed */
  grid-template-rows: 60px 1fr 40px;
  gap: 12px;
}
header, footer { grid-column: 1 / 4; }      /* from line 1 to line 4 = span all 3 columns */

[wk2example23.html]. Key ideas:

  • fr = a fraction of the remaining free space after fixed sizes and gaps. 1fr 3fr gives the first ¼ and the second ¾ [Wk2 slides; CSS Quiz Q3, p8].
  • repeat(4, 1fr) = four equal columns [CSS Quiz Q8].
  • Grid lines are numbered from 1; N columns have N+1 lines. grid-column: 1 / -1 spans all columns, because -1 means "the last line" [CSS Quiz Q8, p17]. grid-column: span 2 spans two tracks (used as .full-width in [LT26 q4_readonly.css]).
  • Named areas make layouts readable [wk2example24.html]:
.page {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 1fr 3fr;
  grid-template-rows: auto 1fr auto;
  grid-template-areas: "header header"
                       "sidebar main"
                       "footer footer";
  gap: 10px;
  min-height: 90vh;
}
header { grid-area: header; }
aside  { grid-area: sidebar; }
main   { grid-area: main; }
footer { grid-area: footer; }
  • Aligning inside the grid (from [CSS Quiz p18 infographic]): align-items (cell contents, cross axis), justify-items (main axis), align-content / justify-content (the whole grid inside the container).

Mixing fr with % overflows: 200px 25% 75% totals 200px + 100%, wider than the container. Use 200px 1fr 3fr instead [CSS Quiz p8 "Percentage pitfall"]. Also, 1fr items will not shrink below their content width unless you use minmax(0, 1fr) [CSS Quiz p8].

Calendar example [LT26 q1.css]: a 7-column by 6-row grid; 1fr seven times gives seven equal day columns.

.calendar-grid {
  display: grid;
  gap: 8px;
  grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr 1fr 1fr 1fr 1fr 1fr;   /* same as repeat(7, 1fr) */
}

Grid: worked fr example and line-number traps

Container 1200px wide, gap: 20px, grid-template-columns: 200px 1fr 3fr;

  1. Reserve the fixed column: 200px.
  2. Remaining space = 1200 − 200 − (20 + 20 gaps) = 960px.
  3. Total fractions = 1fr + 3fr = 4fr.
  4. 1fr = ¼ × 960 = 240px; 3fr = ¾ × 960 = 720px.
  5. Final columns: 200px | 240px | 720px.

Mixing fr with % (for example 200px 25% 75%) overflows, because percentages use the total container width: 200 + 300 + 900 = 1400px in a 1200px container.

Placing items by line number:

.item { grid-column: 2 / 5; }    /* line 2 to line 5 = spans 3 columns; the END line is exclusive */
.item { grid-column: 1 / -1; }   /* -1 = the last line = spans the full width */

Grid lines start at 1, not 0, and N columns have N+1 lines (a 4-column grid has lines 1 to 5).

THEORY.title: Flexbox or Grid?
THEORY.html:
Diagram: decision tree.

What am I laying out?→Items in ONE row or column?
yes→Flexbox: navbar, button group, card row, centring
no, rows AND columns→Grid: page skeleton, dashboard, gallery
Tip: Grid for the page skeleton, Flexbox for components inside it
Flexbox Grid
Dimensions one (row or column) two (rows and columns)
Sizing driven by content (items decide) layout (grid decides)
Best for navbars, toolbars, centring page layouts, dashboards, galleries

[Wk2 slides "Flexbox vs Grid"]. Use both together: in [wk2example23.html] the outer container is a grid and each cell uses flex to centre its text.

THEORY.title: Responsive design
THEORY.html:
Start with the viewport tag in the HTML <head> (without it, mobile browsers render at desktop width and then zoom out):

<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

Mobile-first media queries (base styles are for phones; add complexity upward):

.container { padding: 1rem; }

@media (min-width: 768px) {
  .container { padding: 2rem; display: flex; }
}
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  body { background: #111; color: #eee; }
}

Other tools: max-width: 100% on images, clamp(1rem, 2.5vw, 2rem) for fluid type, relative units.

THEORY.title: Tables
THEORY.html:
table, th, td { border: 1px dashed blue; }        /* size style colour */
table { border-collapse: collapse; width: 50%; }  /* merge the double borders into one */
th, td { padding: 8px; text-align: left; border-bottom: 1px solid grey; }
th { background-color: green; color: white; }
tr:hover { background-color: rgb(185, 206, 185); }   /* row highlight on mouse over */
tr:nth-child(odd) { background-color: rgb(96, 142, 28); }   /* zebra stripes */

[wk2example16.html; Wk2 slides "Table Styling"]. Order matters: in that example tr:nth-child(odd) comes after tr:hover, so on odd rows the stripe colour beats the hover colour (same specificity, later wins).

Truncating long text with an ellipsis [CSS Quiz Q6, p13]. The question asks which property must be set on the <table>: table-layout: fixed;. The infographic also says the cell needs all three of the following:

table { table-layout: fixed; width: 100%; }
td { white-space: nowrap; overflow: hidden; text-overflow: ellipsis; }

THEORY.title: Links and lists
THEORY.html:
a:link    { color: red; }       /* unvisited */
a:visited { color: green; }     /* visited */
a:hover   { color: hotpink; }   /* mouse over */
a:active  { color: blue; }      /* at the moment of click */

[Wk2 slides "Link Properties"; wk2example18.html]. Keep this order (link, visited, hover, active): later rules override earlier ones at equal specificity (added context).

ul.a { list-style-image: url('img.png'); }   /* image as bullet */
ul.b { list-style-type: square; }
ol.c { list-style-type: upper-roman; }       /* also lower-alpha */
ul   { list-style: none; padding: 0; }       /* remove bullets (added context; Bootstrap's list-unstyled does this) */

The slide text swaps the names: <ul> is the unordered list (bullets); <ol> is the ordered list (numbers).

Link-state order mnemonic

Declare link states in "Love-Hate" order: Link, Visited, Hover, Active.

THEORY.title: Styling forms
THEORY.html:
input[type=text] {
  width: 100%;
  padding: 12px 20px 12px 40px;
  margin: 8px 0;
  box-sizing: border-box;              /* stops width:100% + padding overflowing */
  border: 2px solid #ccc;
  border-radius: 4px;
}
select { width: 100%; padding: 16px 20px; border: none; border-radius: 4px; background-color: #f1f1f1; }
input[type=button], input[type=submit], input[type=reset] {
  background-color: #4CAF50; border: none; color: white;
  padding: 16px 32px; margin: 4px 2px; cursor: pointer;      /* hand icon on hover */
}
input:checked { height: 50px; width: 50px; }   /* [marketplace.html] enlarges a ticked box */

[wk2example20.html, wk2example21.html]. The attribute selector input[type=text] targets only text boxes so it does not restyle buttons or checkboxes.

THEORY.title: Custom properties, transitions and animations
THEORY.html:
Custom properties (CSS variables):

:root { --primary: #14b8a6; --radius: 8px; }
.btn { background: var(--primary); border-radius: var(--radius); }
.btn:hover { background: var(--primary, teal); }      /* 2nd argument = fallback */

Transitions (A to B smoothly):

.btn { transition: background-color 0.2s ease, transform 0.2s ease; }
.btn:hover { transform: translateY(-2px); }

Keyframe animations:

@keyframes fade-in { from { opacity: 0; } to { opacity: 1; } }
.modal { animation: fade-in 0.3s ease-out forwards; }

THEORY.title: Pseudo-classes and pseudo-elements
THEORY.html:
Pseudo-class (state) Meaning
:hover / :focus / :active Interaction states
:disabled, :checked, :required, :invalid Form states
:first-child, :last-child, :nth-child(2n) Position
:not(.x) Negation
Pseudo-element (part) Meaning
::before / ::after Inject generated content (needs content: "")
::placeholder, ::first-line, ::selection Parts of an element

Single colon for states, double colon for parts.

THEORY.title: Extra CSS facts
THEORY.html:
• Margin collapsing: vertical margins between adjacent block siblings merge into the larger one (not the sum). It does not happen inside flex or grid containers.
  • rem is relative to the root (html) font-size; ch is the width of the "0" glyph (max-width: 65ch gives readable line lengths).
  • visibility: hidden hides an element but keeps its space; display: none removes it from layout.
  • Inheritance: color, font-*, line-height and text-align pass from parent to child; margin, padding, border and background do not. Force with inherit; reset with initial / unset.

THEORY.title: Bootstrap 5.3 (Week 3)
THEORY.subtitle: Chapter overview
THEORY.html: What it is: "the most popular HTML, CSS, and JS framework for developing responsive, mobile first projects" [Wk3 slides]. In programmer terms, Bootstrap = bootstrap.min.css + bootstrap.min.js. Why it exists: you get a 12-column responsive grid, ready-made components and utility classes, so you write class names instead of CSS rules. When to use it: any time the question says "use Bootstrap", "responsive", "breakpoint", "navbar", "card" or "grid". If the question says vanilla CSS, do not use Bootstrap (Q1) [LT26 Q1 instructions]. In Q2 you may not add custom CSS [LT26 Q2 instructions].

THEORY.title: Installing Bootstrap
THEORY.html:
Option A: CDN in plain HTML [Wk3 slides; wk3example1.html]:

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <!-- REQUIRED for responsiveness on phones -->
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <link href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap@5.3.3/dist/css/bootstrap.min.css" rel="stylesheet">
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Hello, world!</h1>
  <!-- JS bundle (includes Popper) at the END of body: needed for dropdown, collapse, carousel -->
  <script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap@5.3.3/dist/js/bootstrap.bundle.min.js"></script>
</body>
</html>

(The slides also show integrity="sha384-..." and crossorigin="anonymous" attributes on both tags; they are a security check, copy them from getbootstrap.com if you want them.)

Option B: inside a Vue project [Wk5 slides "Using Bootstrap with Vue 3"]:

pnpm add bootstrap

// src/main.js
import 'bootstrap/dist/css/bootstrap.min.css'
import 'bootstrap/dist/js/bootstrap.bundle.min.js'

In the lab test main.js already contains these two imports [LT26 main.js], so Bootstrap classes work in your .vue file immediately. Never add <link> tags in a .vue file.

Bootstrap 4 to 5 renames (added context). Your slides use Bootstrap 5.3, but several solution files in the archive (cssBootstrap/solutions) and older web tutorials use Bootstrap 4 names. In 5.3 the old names do nothing.

Bootstrap 4 (old, wrong in 5.3) Bootstrap 5.3 (use this)
data-toggle, data-target data-bs-toggle, data-bs-target (and data-bs-slide, data-bs-ride)
ml-* / mr-* ms-* / me-* (start / end)
pl-* / pr-* ps-* / pe-*
text-left / text-right text-start / text-end
float-left / float-right float-start / float-end
font-weight-bold, font-italic fw-bold, fst-italic
form-group removed: use spacing such as mb-3
badge-danger badge bg-danger
jumbotron removed: build with utilities (§6.4)
rounded-lg rounded-3
custom-select form-select
sr-only visually-hidden
no-gutters g-0

Slide inconsistency: the Dropdown and Collapse slides say data-toggle="dropdown" and target="#id". The example files correctly use data-bs-toggle and data-bs-target [wk3example10.html, wk3example11.html]. Trust the example files. The Table slide's thead-dark and [wk3example8.html]'s class="thead-dark" are also Bootstrap 4; in 5.3 use table-dark.

The non-bundle JS file (bootstrap.min.js) does not include Popper.js, so dropdowns, tooltips and popovers would need Popper included separately. The bootstrap.bundle file includes it.

THEORY.title: The grid system
THEORY.html:
What: a 12-column, mobile-first flexbox grid with six responsive tiers [Wk3 slides "Grid System"]. Why: layouts that rearrange themselves as the window narrows. Structure: container then row then col.

Diagram: the grid hierarchy.

  • container / container-fluid / container-md
    • row (columns must sit inside a row)
      • col: equal share
      • col-6: 6 of 12 columns
      • col-md-4: 4 of 12 from md upward

Each level is one class on a <div>. Columns inside a row should add up to 12; extra columns wrap to a new line.

Containers [Wk3 slides]:

Class Behaviour
container fixed max-width, resizes in steps at breakpoints, centred
container-fluid 100% width, resizes continuously with the window
container-{bp} (container-lg) 100% wide until that breakpoint, then max-width applies

Breakpoints [Wk3 slides "Breakpoints"]:

Breakpoint Class infix Min width
Extra small (none) < 576px
Small sm ≥ 576px
Medium md ≥ 768px
Large lg ≥ 992px
Extra large xl ≥ 1200px
Extra extra large xxl ≥ 1400px

The Spacing slide says "breakpoint md (720px)". That is the max container width at md. The breakpoint where md starts is 768px, as in the table above and in the lab test (md breakpoint (≥ 768 px) [LT26 Q2]).

Reading a column class: col-{breakpoint}-{n}. It is mobile-first: a class applies from that breakpoint upward, and anything below it stacks full-width.

<div class="container">
  <div class="row">
    <div class="col box"> 1 of 3 </div>            <!-- col = equal share of leftover width -->
    <div class="col-6 box"> 2 of 3 (wider) </div>  <!-- 6 of 12 = half, at every size -->
    <div class="col box"> 3 of 3 </div>
  </div>
</div>

[wk3example3.html]. Breakpoint version [wk3example4.html]:

<div class="row">
  <div class="col-sm-8">...</div>   <!-- stacked below 576px; 8/12 beside the other at >= 576px -->
  <div class="col-sm-4">...</div>
</div>

Layout recipes

Goal Classes Why
50% on tablets (≥768px), full width on phones col-md-6 below md nothing applies, so it stacks [CSS Quiz Q9]; col-sm-6 would go 50% on large phones already
4 equal columns on xl, 3 on md, 2 on small on the row: row-cols-2 row-cols-md-3 row-cols-xl-4, each child col row-cols-* sets columns per row so you do not repeat classes on every cell [LT26 q2.vue]
Different widths at different sizes col-12 col-md-8 col-lg-6 later (larger) breakpoint overrides the smaller one
Centre a column row justify-content-center flex alignment on the row
Space columns apart justify-content-between / around / end [Wk3 slides "Grid Content Alignment"]
Gaps between columns g-3, gx-4 (horizontal), gy-* (vertical) gutters [wk3solutions ex6 album; LT26 q2.vue]
Push a column right offset-md-1 [wk3solutions ex6 album] (added context)
Reorder columns order-1, order-2, order-md-1 needed when the DOM order is not the display order (added context: the 2024 Q2 requires "Thank you text before the Submit button")
Show only on some sizes d-none d-md-block, d-md-none [wk3example13.html carousel caption]

Common grid errors - Columns outside a .row: gutters and widths break. - Using col-sm-* when the question says md. Match the breakpoint named in the question exactly. - Forgetting the small-screen class: col-md-6 alone stacks full-width on phones, which is often what you want; but if you need 2 per line on phones, add col-6. - container inside container (nested) [wk3example3.html] works but wastes width; do not nest without a reason. - Setting justify-content-* on a .col instead of the .row.

Quiz reasoning [CSS Quiz Q10]: at 700px the screen is below md (768px), so only the base and sm (≥576px) classes apply. Ignore col-md-* and col-lg-* when a screen is narrower than those breakpoints.

Worked example: mixed breakpoints at 700px

<div class="container border p-3">
  <div class="row g-2">
    <div class="col-12 col-md-8 col-lg-6 bg-primary text-white p-3">Box A</div>
    <div class="col-6  col-md-4 col-lg-3 bg-secondary text-white p-3">Box B</div>
    <div class="col-6  col-md-12 col-lg-3 bg-success text-white p-3">Box C</div>
  </div>
</div>

At 700px the viewport is above sm but below md (768px), so only the unprefixed classes apply. Box A is col-12 (100%, alone on its row). Box B and Box C are col-6 each (50% + 50% = 100%), so they sit together on the next row. Result: A on row 1; B and C together on row 2.

THEORY.title: Utility classes (styling without CSS)
THEORY.html:
Utilities are one-purpose classes you combine. Docs: getbootstrap.com/docs/5.3/utilities/ [Wk3 slides].

Text [wk3example5.html]

Class Effect
text-center, text-start, text-end alignment
lead larger intro paragraph
mark highlight (<mark> tag or class)
fw-bold, fw-bolder, fw-light, fw-normal weight [wk3solutions, LT26 q2.vue]
fst-italic italic (Q2 Part B: "Use only Bootstrap class(es)" to italicise the subtitle) [LT26 q2.vue]
text-muted, text-white, text-white-50, text-primary/secondary/success/danger/warning/dark text colour
text-decoration-line-through strike-through [LT26 q2.vue]
display-4, display-5, fs-4, small big headings and font sizes [wk3example14.html, LT26 q2.vue]

Colours bg-primary, bg-secondary, bg-success, bg-danger, bg-warning, bg-info, bg-light, bg-dark, bg-white, bg-transparent. The slide combination: class="d-inline p-2 bg-primary text-white" [Wk3 slides "Utilities: Display"].

Spacing [Wk3 slides "Utilities: Spacing"]. Format {property}{sides}-{size} or {property}{sides}-{breakpoint}-{size}.

Part Options
property m margin, p padding
sides t top, b bottom, s start (left), e end (right), x left+right, y top+bottom, none = all four
size 0 to 5, auto (margin only)
breakpoint sm md lg xl xxl (optional)

Examples: mx-auto centres a fixed-width block; px-md-5 = padding left+right size 5 from md upward; mb-3; mt-auto; ms-lg-4. Approximate sizes (added context): 1 = 0.25rem, 2 = 0.5rem, 3 = 1rem, 4 = 1.5rem, 5 = 3rem.

Display d-{value} and d-{bp}-{value}: d-none, d-inline, d-inline-block, d-block, d-flex [Wk3 slides]. d-none d-md-block = hidden below md, shown from md up.

Sizing w-25 w-50 w-75 w-100 w-auto, h-25 h-50 h-75 h-100: relative to the parent [Wk3 slides "Utilities: Sizing"]. h-100 on cards makes all cards in a row equal height [LT26 q2.vue].

Flex utilities: d-flex, flex-column, justify-content-center/between, align-items-center ([wk3solutions album]), for example <form class="d-flex"> for a navbar search box.

Other seen in the files: border, border-dark, border-top-0, rounded-3, rounded-pill, shadow-sm, position-absolute, visually-hidden, list-unstyled.

Images and lists

<img src="a.png" class="img-fluid" height="auto">                   <!-- scales with the container -->
<img src="a.png" class="img-fluid float-start">                     <!-- float-end for right -->
<img src="a.png" class="mx-auto d-block">                           <!-- centre: mx-auto only works on BLOCK elements; img is inline -->
<ul class="list-unstyled"> ... </ul>                                <!-- no bullets -->
<ul class="list-inline"><li class="list-inline-item">..</li></ul>   <!-- one row -->

[wk3example6.html, wk3example7.html]. The comment in [wk3example7.html] explains why: <img> is inline-level, so add d-block before mx-auto can centre it.

More utilities

Category Classes
Theme colours primary (blue), secondary (grey), success (green), danger (red), warning (yellow), info (cyan), light, dark; used as text-*, bg-*, btn-*, border-*, alert-*
Position position-relative, position-absolute, fixed-top, sticky-top, top-0, start-50, translate-middle
Text text-truncate, text-uppercase, fs-1 to fs-6
Visibility visually-hidden (screen-reader only), invisible (hidden but keeps its space)
Background bg-body-tertiary
Colour mode <html data-bs-theme="dark"> (also works on any sub-element)

THEORY.title: Components
THEORY.html:
Components that move (dropdown, collapse, carousel, navbar toggle) need the JS bundle and data-bs-* attributes. Purely visual ones (buttons, cards, badges) need only the CSS.

Buttons

<button type="button" class="btn btn-primary">Primary</button>
<!-- variants: btn-secondary btn-success btn-danger btn-warning btn-info btn-light btn-dark btn-link -->
<a class="btn btn-outline-dark mt-auto" href="#">Outline</a>   <!-- .btn also works on <a> and <input> -->
<button class="btn btn-primary btn-lg">Large</button>           <!-- btn-sm for small -->

<div class="btn-group">                                          <!-- horizontal group -->
  <button type="button" class="btn btn-secondary">Left</button>
  <button type="button" class="btn btn-secondary">Middle</button>
</div>
<div class="btn-group-vertical"> ... </div>                      <!-- vertical group (Exercise 3; added context: not in slide text) -->

[wk3example9.html; Wk3 slides "Buttons"; wk3solutions album uses btn-group-vertical]. Always put btn plus a colour class.

Badges and alerts

<span class="badge bg-danger text-white">Hot!</span>     <!-- red with white text (Q2 Part C) -->
<span class="badge bg-dark text-white">Sale</span>       <!-- black with white text -->
<span class="badge bg-dark rounded-pill">0</span>
<div class="alert alert-warning" role="alert">Input your warning message here.</div>

[LT26 q2.vue; Extra Exercises Vue Basics Q3]. To change a badge from black to red, replace bg-dark with bg-danger only on the "Hot!" badges (Sale badges must stay black).

Tables

Table styling is opt-in: nothing happens until you add .table [Wk3 slides "Table"].

<table class="table table-dark table-borderless table-sm">
  <caption class="text-center">List of users</caption>
  <thead><tr><th scope="col">#</th><th scope="col">Name</th></tr></thead>
  <tbody><tr><th scope="row">1</th><td>Mark</td></tr></tbody>
</table>

Modifiers from the slides: table-dark, table-borderless, table-sm. Common extras (added context): table-striped, table-hover.

Cards

<div class="card" style="width: 18rem;">
  <img src="./img/emo.png" class="card-img-top" alt="...">
  <div class="card-body">
    <h5 class="card-title">Card title</h5>
    <h6 class="card-subtitle mb-2 text-muted">Subtitle</h6>

THEORY.title: Accessibility (WAI-ARIA), the short version
THEORY.html: WAI-ARIA adds attributes (role="alert", aria-label, aria-expanded, aria-controls, aria-hidden) that tell screen readers what elements mean. Browsers do their best with them and ignoring them does not break the page [Wk3 slides "Extra"]. Copy the ones in the examples; do not delete them. Use visually-hidden for text that only screen readers should read.

THEORY.title: Starting from a Bootstrap template
THEORY.html: Download the examples from getbootstrap.com/docs/5.3/examples/, unzip, and customise; for example the album sub-folder is the base for Exercise 6 [Wk3 slides; wk3solutions/ex6/album/ex6-album.html].

THEORY.title: Bootstrap pattern: solving "fix this layout" questions
THEORY.html:
Both lab tests hand you an existing Bootstrap page with a specific bug. The approach:

  1. Find which requirement names a breakpoint (≥768px means md). Translate to the class infix.
  2. Change classes only (Q2: no custom CSS, do not change IDs or text).
  3. Check the smallest screen last: the class without an infix is what small screens get.
Bug Fix Source
Navbar is always a hamburger navbar-expand-md on <nav> [LT26 Q2A]
Subtitle must be italic add fst-italic [LT26 Q2B]
"Hot!" badge should be red bg-dark to bg-danger on that badge only [LT26 Q2C]
Cells always in 3 columns; want 2 / 3 / 4 by width row-cols-2 row-cols-md-3 row-cols-xl-4 on the row [LT26 Q2D]
Two columns of 4 at lg; other widths differ col-lg-4 on #desc and #image, etc. [LT24 Q2A] (approach inferred; screenshots not readable)
Text must come before a button on all sizes order-1 on the text column, order-2 on the button column [LT24 Q2B/C] (added context)
Fields must be 5 of 12 columns at md; 10 of 12 on phones col-md-5 col-10 [LT24 Q2B/C]

THEORY.title: Customising Bootstrap
THEORY.html:
1. Override with your own CSS loaded after Bootstrap (simple, but watch specificity).
  2. CSS variables (v5.3): :root { --bs-primary: #14b8a6; }, or per-component variables such as --bs-btn-bg.
  3. Sass (build projects): override variables before importing Bootstrap, e.g. $primary: #14b8a6;.
  4. Dark mode: <html data-bs-theme="dark">.
  5. Bootstrap Icons is a separate package: <i class="bi bi-heart"></i>.

THEORY.title: Using Bootstrap inside a Vue project
THEORY.html:
Install and import as shown in section 6.1 (Option B). Then:

  • Bootstrap classes work directly in <template>; bind them dynamically with :class (section 7.8).
  • <style scoped> will not affect Bootstrap's own classes inside child components; prefer utility classes or CSS variables to tweak them.
  • For heavy interactivity, consider bootstrap-vue-next (Vue-native components) rather than mixing Bootstrap's DOM-driven JS with Vue's rendering. Do not let Bootstrap JS and Vue both manage the same element's DOM.

THEORY.title: Why Vue exists: the problem with the DOM
THEORY.html:
The browser turns HTML into the DOM, a tree of objects JavaScript can change (document.getElementById(...)). That works until many elements depend on the same data. The slides' example: add one item to a Shopee cart and the count, total, shipping and checkout button all change. With vanilla JS "who is responsible for keeping all of those DOM elements synchronized? Answer: us." [Wk4 slides "DOM Manipulation"].

A reactive app observes changes in state, propagates the change, and re-renders the view automatically. You describe what the UI should look like for a given state (declarative); Vue handles how to update the DOM [Wk4 slides "What is a Reactive Application?"].

Diagram: the reactive loop.

State: ref() valuesVue tracks reads →Template: {{ }} and v-directivesrenders →DOM on screen
DOM on screenuser event: @click, v-model →Handler changes state.valueback to →State: ref() values

Read it as a cycle: you never touch the DOM; you only change .value, and the template re-renders. The Wk4 take-away: "no more document.getElement...".

Imperative vs declarative, side by side

Imperative (vanilla JavaScript) Declarative (reactivity, e.g. Vue)
You tell the browser... How to update the DOM, step by step What the UI should look like for a given state
Example (user logs in) document.querySelector('#message').textContent = 'Welcome, ' + username, then separately hide the login button, then update other UI pieces, one line per DOM node <p v-if="loggedIn">Welcome, {{ username }}!</p><button v-else>Login</button>
Who keeps the UI in sync? You, manually, in every place state can change The framework: it detects the change and updates everything that depends on it
As the app grows Many places to update (easy to forget one); repetitive code; UI logic scattered; hard to scale; tightly coupled to the DOM structure One source of truth; UI always in sync; less code; logic lives with the data; scales naturally

Key takeaway: imperative = you change the DOM step by step (more control, more work, more room for bugs). Declarative/reactive = you change the state and the UI follows automatically. This is the biggest conceptual shift in the course and the reason Vue (and every modern frontend framework) exists.

The smallest example. Without a framework, if score changes you must find the HTML that displays it and update it every time:

document.getElementById("score").textContent = score;

Vue removes this step:

<p>{{ score }}</p>   <!-- changing `score` updates this line automatically -->

Why use a framework rather than plain JavaScript? A single static page can be built without one. Vue becomes useful once a page has many interdependent parts, because it removes the repetitive task of locating and updating each piece of HTML manually.

What Vue is

"Vue (pronounced like View) is a progressive framework for building user interfaces. The core library is focused on the view layer only, and is easy to pick up and integrate with other libraries or existing projects. On the other hand, Vue is also perfectly capable of powering sophisticated Single-Page Applications when used in combination with modern tooling and supporting libraries."

Framework Backed by / used by
Vue.js Used by Alibaba
Angular Google
React Facebook (Meta)

Selling points: extremely small (~16KB core), great runtime performance, easy to learn. React has historically led in raw npm dependents, but Vue is consistently the second most popular JavaScript framework.

Feature What it does
Data binding Assign values to HTML attributes, styles and classes via v-bind
Directives Built-in special attributes (v-if, v-else, v-on, v-bind, v-model, ...) that perform actions on the rendered DOM
Event handling v-on listens for DOM events
Computed properties Automatically recalculate derived values when the data they depend on changes
Components Custom, reusable elements that behave like your own HTML tags (section 7.14)

Components, a first look. Components build a large application out of small, self-contained, reusable pieces, each a template bundled with its own Vue logic under one name. A large app is a tree of nested components (a root <div id="app"> containing an <app-nav>, an <app-view> that itself contains <app-sidebar> and <app-content>), mirroring how native HTML elements nest.

THEORY.title: Setting up a Vue project
THEORY.html:
Prerequisites [Wk4 slides "Install"]: Node.js ≥ 22.12.0 (node -v), then pnpm (npm install -g pnpm, check with pnpm -v). VS Code extension Vue (Official) (vue.volar) and Chrome Vue.js devtools.

pnpm create vue@latest
#   Project name    -> vue-example
#   TypeScript?     -> No
#   Features (space bar to select): Router, Pinia, Vitest, End-to-End Testing, Linter, Prettier
#   E2E framework   -> Playwright
#   Experimental    -> none
#   Skip example code? -> No
cd vue-example
pnpm install
pnpm format
pnpm dev          # open the localhost link; Ctrl+C stops the server
pnpm add bootstrap   # Wk5: styling
pnpm add axios       # Wk5: HTTP

[Wk4 slides "Quick Start (1) to (3)"; Wk5 slides]. In the lab test the projects arrive pre-made: you run pnpm install then pnpm dev (§13).

Project layout [Wk4 slides "Structure of a Vue App"; wk4examples]:

vue-example/
|-- index.html            the ONLY html page (SPA); has <div id="app"></div> and loads /src/main.js
|-- package.json          dependencies + scripts (dev, build, format ...)
|-- vite.config.js        bundler config (rarely touched)
|-- public/               static files copied as-is (favicon, assets/wad.png), referenced as /assets/wad.png
`-- src/
    |-- main.js           creates the app, installs router/pinia, mounts on #app
    |-- App.vue           root component: usually just <RouterView />
    |-- assets/           files processed by the bundler (css, images), referenced like ../assets/me.png
    |-- components/       reusable UI pieces (NavBar.vue, PostCard.vue ...)
    |-- views/            route-level pages (HomeView.vue) that have a URL
    |-- router/index.js   maps URL paths to components
    `-- stores/           Pinia state (Appendix A)

src/main.js [wk5 example main.js]:

import { createApp } from 'vue'
import { createPinia } from 'pinia'
import App from './App.vue'
import router from './router'
import 'bootstrap/dist/css/bootstrap.min.css'
import 'bootstrap/dist/js/bootstrap.bundle.min.js'

const app = createApp(App)
app.use(createPinia())
app.use(router)
app.mount('#app')          // attaches App to <div id="app"> in index.html

src/App.vue [wk4examples App.vue]:

<script setup>
// import { RouterLink, RouterView } from 'vue-router'
</script>
<template>
  <RouterView />        <!-- the current route's component appears here -->
</template>

src/assets vs public [Wk4 slides]:

src/assets/ public/
Reference with relative path ../assets/logo.png or /src/assets/me.png web-root path /assets/wad.png
Build compiled, optimised, minified copied as-is
Unused files dropped from the build all included 
<script setup>
import { ref } from 'vue'
import wad from '/assets/wad.png'              // method A: file in public/assets
const me = ref('/src/assets/me.png')           // method B: file in src/assets
</script>
<template>
  <img v-bind:src="wad">
  <img v-bind:src="me">
  <img src="../assets/me.png" :width="200">    <!-- static path is fine too -->
</template>

[wk4examples Example5.vue].

Setup details

  • Editor: install the Vue (Official) extension (formerly vue.volar) in VS Code for syntax highlighting, auto-completion, type checking, real-time diagnostics and refactoring of .vue files. In Chrome, install Vue.js devtools to inspect the component tree, reactive state and routing.
  • Node.js (from https://nodejs.org/en) ships with npm. Check with node -v (need ≥ 22.12.0).
  • pnpm ("Performant npm") is a fast, disk-efficient drop-in replacement for npm/Yarn. It uses a global content-addressable store and links packages into projects with hard links/symlinks instead of duplicating them. Install with npm install -g pnpm; verify with pnpm -v.
  • pnpm install downloads the packages the project depends on. pnpm format runs Prettier. pnpm dev starts the Vite dev server and prints a URL, usually http://localhost:5173/. Ctrl+C stops it; run pnpm dev again to restart.
  • The link containing /__devtools__/ opens the Vue dev console (an alternative to the Chrome extension). Press Alt+Shift+D inside the running app to toggle it.

The rest of the scaffold

Path What it is
e2e/ Playwright end-to-end test specs
node_modules/ External libraries, auto-generated, never edit directly
vite.config.js Vite bundler config (plugins, proxies, build options)
vitest.config.ts Vitest, a Vite-native unit/component testing framework (.ts = TypeScript, a typed superset of JS compiled down to JS)
playwright.config.js Playwright, an end-to-end (E2E) testing framework that launches real browsers to simulate whole user journeys (login, clicking, checkout), as opposed to unit tests of small isolated pieces
stores/ Pinia state-management logic (centralised cross-app data)
views/ (or pages/) Full-page components mapped to routes (Home.vue, About.vue)
utils/ (your own) Optional folder for shared helpers (date formatters, calculators)

How the three entry files fit together:

  • index.html contains <div id="app"></div>, the mount point where all Vue-rendered content is injected, and imports main.js.
  • main.js imports your libraries and root component, creates the Vue app instance and mounts it on that <div id="app">.
  • App.vue is the root component that every other component is (directly or indirectly) nested inside.

The test tooling is present as default scaffolding; the syllabus places "Unit, Integration, E2E Testing" in Week 10, so in Weeks 4 to 6 it is not yet the focus.

THEORY.title: The Single-File Component (SFC)
THEORY.html:
What: one .vue file holds the three things a page needs: JavaScript, HTML and CSS [Wk4 slides "Component: Syntax"].

<script setup>
  // JS: imports, data, functions
</script>

<template>
  <!-- HTML with Vue syntax. Vue 3 allows several root elements -->
</template>

<style scoped>
  /* CSS: "scoped" = applies to THIS component only */
</style>
  • <script setup> runs for each component instance. Everything you declare at the top level (variables, functions, imports) is usable in the template automatically.
  • defineProps and defineEmits are compiler macros: use them without importing (§7.14).
  • To use external CSS in a component: import './q1.css' inside <script setup> [LT26 q1.vue].
  • Lab-test files begin with a /* Name / Email */ comment, and .vue files may also use <!-- --> [LT26 Instructions; LT24 q1.vue].

<style scope> is not <style scoped>. [wk4examples MainMenu.vue] has the typo scope, so that style is not scoped. Also, scoped CSS will not style child components' inner elements.

The three blocks, in a table

Block Description
<template> The component's HTML
<script setup> The component's data and logic
<style> The component's CSS

A component does not require all three blocks. A component with no reactive data can omit <script setup>, and one that relies on inherited or global styling can omit <style>. <template> is the only block every component requires, since without it there is nothing to render.

  • <template> holds the HTML the component renders. Alongside standard HTML it supports directives and components. {{ }} evaluates a single JavaScript expression and displays the result as text, updating whenever the data it depends on changes.
  • <script setup> is regular JavaScript. Anything declared here (a variable, a function, an import) becomes automatically available to the template, with no extra step linking the two. import { ref } from 'vue' imports the function that creates reactive state: data the template continues to watch for changes.
  • <style>: without scoped, the CSS applies to the entire application (an h1 rule would affect every h1). With scoped, Vue rewrites the CSS so it applies only to elements inside this component's own template.
<style scoped>
/* only affects h1s inside this file */
h1 { color: teal; }
</style>

<style>
/* affects every h1 in the whole application */
h1 { color: teal; }
</style>

Use scoped by default. As an application grows to many components, unscoped styles are a common source of one component's CSS unintentionally affecting another.

THEORY.title: Reactive state with ref
THEORY.html:
ref() creates a reactive variable: it wraps your value in an object with a .value property; when .value changes, everything using it re-renders [Wk4 slides "Component: Syntax"].

<script setup>
import { ref } from 'vue'                 // 1. import
const name = ref("John")                  // 2. define data
const phone = ref(123456)
console.log(name.value)                   // 3. in JS you MUST use .value
function getPhone() {                     // 4. methods are plain functions
  return "This is my number " + phone.value
}
</script>

<template>
  <h1>Name : {{ name }}</h1>              <!-- in the template, NO .value -->
  <h1>Phone : {{ getPhone() }}</h1>
</template>

[wk4examples Example2.vue].

Rule Detail
Script needs .value, template does not count.value++ in JS; {{ count }} in HTML
Arrays / objects const items = ref([]), then items.value.push(x), items.value.splice(i, 1) [Ex4.vue wk5]
Not reactive a plain const boolean_seen = true will not update the page; wrap it: ref(boolean_seen) [wk4examples Example3.vue]
reactive() a second way for objects; the slides mention it but do not use it, use ref
Debug select the component in Vue devtools and edit a value to watch the page update [Wk4 slides "Data Binding (2)"]

State, const and reactive

State: data that drives an application, stored in a form that Vue can watch for changes. It is the data a component holds in memory between renders (a counter, a list of items, a boolean flag for whether a menu is open). What distinguishes state from an ordinary variable is that Vue actively watches it and re-renders any part of the template that depends on it.

ref(0) returns an object with a single property, .value, currently holding 0. Vue watches this object, and any change to .value is detected automatically.

const count = ref(0)

console.log(count)         // { value: 0 } (plus some internal properties)
console.log(count.value)   // 0
count.value = count.value + 1
console.log(count.value)   // 1

Inside a <template>, top-level refs are unwrapped automatically, so you write {{ count }}.

Why const works. If count is const, how can its value change?

const count = ref(0)

count.value = 5     // OK: mutating the .value property of the existing object
count = ref(10)     // ERROR: count cannot be reassigned

const only prevents the variable from being pointed at a different object; it says nothing about the contents of the object. The binding never needs to change, only the value stored inside it, which is why const is the convention for ref.

reactive makes an object deeply reactive without .value:

import { reactive } from 'vue'
const user = reactive({ name: 'John', role: 'Engineer' })
user.name = 'Jane'   // reactive, no .value needed

Caveats: it only works for objects (not primitives), and you lose reactivity if you reassign the whole variable or destructure it. Many developers use ref for everything.

THEORY.title: Interpolation and expressions
THEORY.html:
{{ ... }} ("mustache") inserts a JavaScript expression result as text.

{{ name }}  {{ getPhone() }}  {{ 'Mr ' + name }}  {{ 1 + 2 }}  {{ name.toUpperCase() }}
{{ number + 1 }}    {{ ok ? 'YES' : 'NO' }}    {{ message.split('').reverse().join('') }}
<div :id="`list-${id}`"></div>

[wk4 Example2.vue; wk5 Example2.vue].

Expressions only [Wk5 slides "Using JavaScript Expressions (2)"]: an expression is anything that can go after return. Statements do not work.

{{ var a = 1 }}                          <!-- WRONG: statement -->
{{ if (ok) { return message } }}         <!-- WRONG: flow control; use a ternary -->
{{ ok ? message : '' }}                  <!-- RIGHT -->
  • Mustaches cannot go inside an HTML attribute. <img src="{{ url }}"> is wrong; use :src="url" (§7.8) [Wk4 slides "Attribute Binding (1)"].
  • v-html renders a string as raw HTML. The lab tests penalise unnecessary v-html by 1 mark per occurrence [LT26 Instructions]. Use {{ }} for text; v-html only when you really must show HTML markup (the slide examples use it for prod.desc that contains <p> tags).

Expressions, statements and v-html in detail

  • Expression: a piece of code that produces a value, e.g. score + 1.
  • Statement: a piece of code that performs an action but does not produce a value, e.g. if (score > 50) { console.log('Pass') }.

{{ }} evaluates a single expression and inserts the result as text. By default it escapes its result, so HTML tags are shown literally:

<script setup>
import { ref } from 'vue'
const message = ref('<em>Warning</em>')
</script>

<template>
  <p>{{ message }}</p>           <!-- shows the literal text  <em>Warning</em>  -->
  <p v-html="message"></p>       <!-- parsed as HTML: italic Warning -->
</template>

Security: cross-site scripting (XSS). v-html inserts a value as raw HTML. If message contains content typed by a user, they can insert their own HTML and JavaScript into the page. {{ }}'s default escaping exists specifically to prevent this. Use v-html only when the source is fully trusted, never on unvalidated user input.

THEORY.title: Directive overview
THEORY.html:
Directives are attributes with a v- prefix. They apply effects to the DOM when the value of their expression changes [Wk4 slides "Vue Directives"].

Directive Shorthand Does Section
v-bind:attr="x" :attr="x" bind an attribute, class or style to a variable §7.8
v-on:event="x" @event="x" listen to a DOM or custom event §7.9
v-model="x" none two-way binding of a form input to a variable §7.10
v-if / v-else-if / v-else none insert or remove an element §7.7
v-for="item in items" none repeat an element per item §7.11
v-html="x" none render a string as HTML (avoid) §7.5
v-slot:name #name (added context) fill a named slot §7.14

Diagram: choosing the right tool.

I need to…Use
Show or hide somethingv-if / v-else
Repeat per array itemv-for + :key
Set an attribute, class or stylev-bind or :
React to click / key / mousev-on or @
Read a form inputv-model
Value derived from other datacomputed()
Side effect when data changeswatch()
Run code once on loadonMounted()

Ask the questions in any order; each answer gives one tool. Most lab questions combine three or four of these.

THEORY.title: Conditional rendering: v-if, v-else-if, v-else
THEORY.html:
What / when: the element is inserted or removed from the DOM depending on a truthy expression. Use it for "show X only when Y", empty-list messages and error banners [Wk4 slides "Conditional Rendering"].

<p v-if="x == 1">Now you see me</p>
<p v-else-if="x == 2">Second case</p>
<p v-else>You don't see me</p>

<!-- toggle several elements at once: <template> is an invisible wrapper, it is NOT rendered -->
<template v-if="ok">
  <h1>Title</h1>
  <p>Paragraph 1</p>
</template>
<template v-else>
  <p>Now you don't</p>
</template>

[wk4 Example3.vue, Example4.vue; wk5 Ex2.vue solution].

  • v-else must come immediately after its v-if or v-else-if element, or Vue does not recognise it.
  • The condition must be a reactive variable to update [Wk4 slides].
  • v-if vs v-show (added context): v-show only toggles CSS display:none; v-if really adds/removes. Prefer v-if (it is what the course uses).

Empty-list pattern (2026 Q3 Part C) [LT26 q3.vue]:

<p v-if="collectionLogs.length === 0">No collection records yet</p>
<table v-else> ... </table>

v-if vs v-show

v-if v-show
Element when the condition is false Removed from the page entirely Present, but hidden with display: none
Cost of toggling Recreates the element each time Only toggles a CSS property
Supports v-else Yes No
Best suited to Content that rarely changes visibility Content that toggles visibility frequently

A v-else-if chain is checked top to bottom and only the first true branch renders. With score = 72 in v-if="score >= 90" (Distinction) / v-else-if="score >= 70" (Merit) / v-else-if="score >= 50" (Pass) / v-else (Fail), the Merit branch renders and the rest are not evaluated further. If another element sits between a v-if and its v-else, Vue cannot associate the two and reports an error.

THEORY.title: Binding attributes, classes and styles: v-bind / :
THEORY.html:
What / when: anywhere an HTML attribute's value should come from a variable: src, href, id, width, value, disabled, class, style. Shorthand : is the norm [Wk4 slides "Attribute Binding"].

<img v-bind:src="myImg" :width="width" :height="height" />

<!-- bind several attributes with ONE object -->
<script setup>
const obj = ref({ width: 200, height: 200, src: '/assets/me.png' })
</script>
<img v-bind="obj" />

[wk4 Ex2.vue solution].

Boolean attributes (disabled, checked) exist by presence. Bind them to a true/false:

<button :disabled="isButtonDisabled">Log In</button>
<input type="checkbox" v-bind:checked="isChecked">
<!-- disable a button until BOTH inputs are filled (2026 Q3 idea) -->
<button :disabled="studentName.trim() === '' || selectedSize === ''">Collect</button>

[wk4 Example6.vue; LT26 q3.vue].

Class binding [wk4 Example8.vue]. Notice the quotes around class names containing a hyphen ('text-danger'), because a hyphen is a minus sign in JavaScript.

<!-- Object: key = class name, value = condition -->
<p :class="{ active: isActive, 'text-danger': hasError }">{{ message }}</p>

<!-- Static + dynamic mix -->
<div class="static" :class="{ demo: isActive, 'text-danger': hasError }"></div>

<!-- Array: apply a list of class names held in variables -->
<div :class="[activeClass, errorClass]"></div>

<!-- Computed object (wk5 Example6.vue) -->
const classObject = computed(() => ({ active: isActive.value && !error.value, 'text-danger': error.value }))
<div :class="classObject">Example</div>

<!-- Two-way switch between two classes (wk4 Ex4.vue solution) -->
<div :class="{ blueBox: blueBox, redBox: !blueBox }"></div>
<button :class="{ btn: true, 'btn-primary': blueBtn, 'btn-danger': !blueBtn }"></button>

Yes/No coloured cells (2026 Q4 Part D) use the same idea with the given classes:

<td :class="course.coreForIS ? 'text-yes' : 'text-no'">{{ course.coreForIS ? 'Yes' : 'No' }}</td>

Style binding takes an object of CSS properties. Use camelCase (fontSize) or quoted kebab ('font-size') [wk4 Example9.vue]:

<p :style="{ color: activeColor, fontSize: size }">Inline styling</p>
<div :style="{ color: activeColor, fontSize: fontSize + 'px' }"></div>   <!-- numbers need units -->
<div :style="{ 'font-size': fontSize + 'em' }">                          <!-- [wk6 Example5View.vue] -->

Ordinary, boolean and merged bindings

Template Result
