Grid areas + CSS Grid — ex7wk2solutions/Ex7/ex7.css

  * { box-sizing: border-box; }
  body { font-family: Arial, sans-serif; margin: 0; color: #1f2937; }

  /* ===========================================================
     PART 1 — GRID (2-column layout with sidebar)
     =========================================================== */
  .page {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-columns: 1fr 2fr;
    grid-template-rows: 80px 1fr;
    grid-template-areas:
      "nav  nav"
      "side main";
    min-height: 100vh;
  }

  nav       { grid-area: nav; background: #18212f; }
  aside     { grid-area: side; background: #f3f4f6; padding: 16px; }
  main      { grid-area: main; padding: 16px; }

  /* ===========================================================
     PART 2 — FLEXBOX (nav bar)
     =========================================================== */
  nav {
    display: flex;
    justify-content: space-between;
    align-items: center;
    padding: 12px 20px;
    color: white;
  }
  nav .logo { font-weight: bold; }
  nav ul { list-style: none; margin: 0; padding: 0; display: flex; gap: 16px; }
  nav a { color: white; text-decoration: none; }

  /* ===========================================================
     PART 3 — FLEXBOX (card row)
     =========================================================== */
  .card-row {
    display: flex;
    justify-content: space-around;
    gap: 12px;
    margin-top: 16px;
  }
  .card {
    width: 300px;
    background: white;
    border: 1px solid #e5e7eb;
    border-radius: 8px;
    padding: 16px;
    min-width: 140px;
  }

Class binding + Style binding — Ex4wk4solutions/Ex4.vue

first comment: Bind the div ID and choose either blueBox or redBox based on blueBox's value.

<script setup>
    // Import ref so values can reactively update the template when they change.
    import { ref } from 'vue'

    // Part 1: store the box ID and whether the box and button should use blue styling.
    const id = ref('demo')
    const blueBox = ref(true)
    const blueBtn = ref(true)

    // Part 2: store the text ID, its current color, and whether the danger button is shown.
    const id2 = ref('demo2')
    const activeColor = ref('red')
    const redBtn = ref(true)

    // Toggle the box between blue and red styling and toggle the matching button style.
    function changeColor() {
        // ref values are read and changed through their .value property in JavaScript.
        if (blueBox.value) {
            blueBox.value = false
            blueBtn.value = false
        } else {
            blueBox.value = true
            blueBtn.value = true
        }
    }

    // Toggle the text color between red and blue and update the button class accordingly.
    function changeTextColor() {
        // Check the current color before choosing the next color.
        if (activeColor.value == "blue") {
            activeColor.value = "red"
            redBtn.value = true
        } else {
            activeColor.value = "blue"
            redBtn.value = false
        }
    }

</script>

<template>
    <!-- Class names containing hyphens must be quoted because a hyphen is an operator in JavaScript. -->
    <div id="part1">
        <!-- Bind the div ID and choose either blueBox or redBox based on blueBox's value. -->
        <div v-bind:id="id" class="m-2" v-bind:class="{'blueBox': blueBox, 'redBox': !blueBox}">
            div ID : {{id}}
        </div>

        <!-- Always apply btn, then choose the button color from the blueBtn value. -->
        <!-- @click calls changeColor whenever the user clicks the button. -->
        <button type="button" v-bind:class="{'btn' : true, 'btn-primary': blueBtn, 'btn-danger': !blueBtn}" @click="changeColor">Change Color</button>
    </div>

    <div id="part2">
        <!-- Bind the second div ID and set its text color from the activeColor value. -->
        <div v-bind:id="id2" class="m-2" v-bind:style="{'color':activeColor}">
            div ID : {{id2}}
        </div>

        <!-- Always apply btn, then choose the button color from the redBtn value. -->
        <!-- @click calls changeTextColor so the text and button change together. -->
        <button type="button" v-bind:class="{'btn' : true, 'btn-primary': !redBtn, 'btn-danger': redBtn}" @click="changeTextColor">Change Text Color</button>
    </div>

</template>

<style scoped>
    /* Give the box a red background when the redBox class is active. */
    .redBox {
            background-color: red;
    }

    /* Give the box a blue background when the blueBox class is active. */
    .blueBox {
        background-color: blue;
    }

    /* Style a primary button with a blue background and white text. */
    .btn-primary {
        background-color: blue;
        color: white;
    }

    /* Style a danger button with a red background and white text. */
    .btn-danger {
        background-color: red;
        color: white;
    }

    /* Make the text inside the first demo white. */
    #demo {
        color: white;
    }
</style>

<script setup>
import { ref } from 'vue'

const counter = ref(0)
const name = ref('Vue')

function hello(event) {
  alert('Hello ' + name.value + '!')
  // `event` is the native DOM event
  // readily available to Vue
  alert(event.target.tagName + ' event!') // -> button event!
}

function say(message) {
  alert(message)
}
</script>

<template>
  <!-- Listening to Events -->
  <button v-on:click="counter += 1">Add 1</button>
  <p>The button above has been clicked {{ counter }} times.</p>

  <button v-on:click="hello">Say Hello</button>

  <button @click="say('hi')">Say hi</button>
  <button @click="say('what')">Say what</button>
  <br /><br />
  Input something and press 'Enter' to trigger the event:
  <input type="text" v-on:keyup.enter="say('You pressed enter!')" />
</template>

computed + Class binding — Example6wk5examples/Example6.vue

<script setup>
import { ref, computed } from 'vue'

const isActive = ref(true)
const error = ref(true)

// computed() recalculates the class object whenever isActive or error changes.
// Vue uses the returned object as class names: each key is added when its value is true.
const classObject = computed(() => ({
  // Add "active" only when the component is active and has no error.
  active: isActive.value && !error.value,
  // Add "text-danger" whenever there is an error.
  'text-danger': error.value,
}))
</script>

<template>
  <div :class="classObject">Example 6</div>
</template>

<style scoped>
.active {
  background-color: lightgray;
}

.text-danger {
  color: red;
}
</style>

<script setup>
import axios from 'axios'
import { ref } from 'vue'

const API_URL = 'https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather'

const weatherData = ref('')
const temperature = ref('')
const status = ref('Ready to fetch weather data')

async function getData() {
  const query = 'Singapore,sg'
  const key = '8d6f21e5351582a8051551f99ef3fa88'

  // Show that we're starting the request
  console.log('Request initiated at:', new Date().toLocaleTimeString())

  try {
    // Make the asynchronous request with await
    const response = await axios.get(API_URL, {
      params: {
        q: query,
        APPID: key,
        units: 'metric',
      },
    })

    console.log('Response received at:', new Date().toLocaleTimeString())

    weatherData.value = response.data.weather[0].description
    temperature.value = response.data.main.temp
    // Update status
    status.value = 'Data received successfully!'
  } catch (error) {
    console.log('Error occurred at:', new Date().toLocaleTimeString())
    status.value = 'Error fetching data!'
    weatherData.value = error.message
  }
}
</script>

<template>
  <div>
    <p id="status">{{ status }}</p>
    <div id="weather">
      <div class="weather-line">
        Current weather in Singapore: <strong>{{ weatherData }}</strong>
      </div>
      <div class="weather-line">
        Temperature: <strong>{{ temperature }}°C</strong>
      </div>
    </div>
    <button type="button" @click="getData">Get Weather Data</button>
  </div>
</template>

<style scoped>
#status {
  color: blue;
  font-weight: bold;
  margin: 10px 0;
}

#weather {
  color: green;
  margin: 10px 0;
}

.interrupt {
  color: red;
}

  margin-bottom: 5px;
}
</style>

<script setup>
import { ref, onMounted } from 'vue'
import axios from 'axios'

const API_URL = 'http://localhost:8000/posts'

const posts = ref([]) // array of post objects
const newEntry = ref('') // new entry to update the post
const newMood = ref('')
const toUpdate = ref(null) // the post object to update
const status = ref('')

onMounted(getPosts)

async function getPosts() {
  try {
    const response = await axios.get(API_URL)
    // this gets the data, which is an array, and pass the data to Vue instance's posts property
    console.log(response.data)
    posts.value = response.data
  } catch (error) {
    posts.value = [{ entry: 'There was an error: ' + error.message }]
  }
}

async function updatePost(id, subject) {
  try {
    const url = `${API_URL}/${id}`

    const response = await axios.put(url, {
      subject: subject,
      entry: newEntry.value,
      mood: newMood.value
    })

    status.value = 'Update Successful'
    console.log(response.data)

    toUpdate.value = null

  } catch (error) {
    status.value = 'There was an error: ' + error.message
    console.log('There was an error: ' + error.message)
  }

  await getPosts() // refresh the posts after update

}
</script>

<template>

  <p v-if="status!=''">{{ status }}</p>
  <table class="table">

        <th>Mood</th>

<script setup>
import { ref, onMounted } from 'vue'

const API_URL = 'http://localhost:8000/posts'

const posts = ref([]) // array of post objects

async function loadData() {

    console.log(response.data)
    posts.value = response.data
  } catch (error) {
    posts.value = [{ entry: 'There was an error: ' + error.message }]
  }
}
onMounted(loadData)

async function deletePost(id, subject) {
    console.log('Subject to delete: ' + subject)
    let idx = 0
    for (let post of posts.value) {
        if (post.subject == subject) {
            posts.value.splice(idx,1) // remove this element
            console.log(posts.value)
            break
        }
        idx++
    }

    try {
        const url = `${API_URL}/${id}`

        // Payload must be inside the 'data' property
        const response = await axios.delete(url, { data: { subject: subject } })

        console.log(response.data)

    } catch (error) {
        console.log('There was an error: ' + error.message)
    }

}
</script>

<template>
  <h2>Blog Posts</h2>

<script setup>
import { ref } from 'vue'

const teamA = ref("Falcons")
const teamB = ref("Tigers")
const scoreA = ref(0)
const scoreB = ref(0)
const step = ref(1) // points added per click
const maxScore = ref(10)

function addA() {
    scoreA.value = Math.min(maxScore.value, scoreA.value + step.value);
}

function addB() {
    scoreB.value = Math.min(maxScore.value, scoreB.value + step.value);
}

function reset() {
    scoreA.value = 0;
    scoreB.value = 0;
}

</script>

<template>

    <div style="font-family: Arial; max-width: 520px; margin: 24px auto;">
        <h2>Mini Scoreboard</h2>

        <p><strong>{{ teamA }}</strong> vs <strong>{{ teamB }}</strong></p>

        <p>Current: {{ scoreA }} - {{ scoreB }}</p>

        <!-- B. In-template expressions go here -->
        <p>Total points: {{ scoreA + scoreB }}</p>

        <p>
            Points left to win:
            {{ maxScore - (scoreA > scoreB ? scoreA : scoreB) }}
        </p>

        <!-- A. Event handlers go here -->
        <div style="display: flex; gap: 12px; margin: 12px 0;">
            <button @click="addA">+ Team A</button>
            <button @click="addB">+ Team B</button>
            <button @click="reset">Reset</button>
        </div>


        <div style="margin-top: 14px;">
            <!-- C. Display winner / status here -->
            <p v-if="scoreA === maxScore">Winner: {{ teamA.toUpperCase() }}</p>
            <p v-else-if="scoreB === maxScore">Winner: {{ teamB + '!' }}</p>

<script setup>
import { ref, computed } from 'vue'

const x = ref(0)
const y = ref(0)
const lastResult = ref(0)
const operators = ref(["+", "-", "*", "/", "%"])
const selectedOp = ref("+")

const result = computed(() => {
    if (selectedOp.value == "+")
        lastResult.value = x.value + y.value;
    else if (selectedOp.value == "-")
        lastResult.value = x.value - y.value;
    else if (selectedOp.value == "*")
        lastResult.value = x.value * y.value;
    else if (selectedOp.value == "/")
        lastResult.value = x.value / y.value;
    else if (selectedOp.value == "%")
        lastResult.value = x.value % y.value;

    return lastResult.value;
})

</script>

<template>
    <p>x <input v-model.number="x"></p>
    <select v-model="selectedOp">
        <option v-for="op in operators">{{ op }}</option>
    </select>
    <p>y <input v-model.number="y"></p>

    <p>---------------------</p>

<script setup>
import { ref, watch } from 'vue'

import axios from 'axios'

const API_URL = 'https://yesno.wtf/api'

const question = ref('')
const answer = ref('Questions usually contain a question mark. ;-)')
const loading = ref(false)

// watch works directly on a ref
async function getAnswer(newQuestion) {
  if (newQuestion.includes('?')) {
    loading.value = true
    answer.value = 'Thinking...'
    try {
      const response = await axios.get(API_URL)
      answer.value = response.data.answer
    } catch (error) {
      answer.value = 'Error! Could not reach the API. ' + error
    } finally {
      loading.value = false
    }
  }
}
watch(question, getAnswer)
</script>

<template>
  <p>
    Ask a yes/no question:
    <input v-model="question" :disabled="loading" />
  </p>
  <p>{{ answer }}</p>
</template>

<script setup>
import { ref, computed, onMounted } from 'vue'
import SettingPanel from '../components/SettingPanel.vue'

const STORAGE_KEY = 'settings'
const theme = ref('light')
const fontSize = ref(16)

function applySettings(newSettings) {
  // basic validation (optional but good)
  if (newSettings.theme === 'light' || newSettings.theme === 'dark') {
    theme.value = newSettings.theme
  }
  if (typeof newSettings.fontSize === 'number') {
    fontSize.value = Math.min(24, Math.max(12, newSettings.fontSize))
  }
}

onMounted(() => {
  const saved = localStorage.getItem(STORAGE_KEY)
  if (saved === null) return

  applySettings(JSON.parse(saved))
})

<script setup>
import { ref, onMounted } from 'vue'

// TODO: Add Code Here to define the props and the emits for the SettingPanel component
const STORAGE_KEY = 'settings'

const theme = ref('light')
const fontSize = ref(16)

const emit = defineEmits(['settings-changed'])

function loadSettings() {
  const saved = localStorage.getItem(STORAGE_KEY)
  if (saved === null) return

  const settings = JSON.parse(saved)
  if (settings.theme === 'light' || settings.theme === 'dark') {
    theme.value = settings.theme
  }
  if (typeof settings.fontSize === 'number') {
    fontSize.value = Math.min(24, Math.max(12, settings.fontSize))
  }
  emit('settings-changed', { theme: theme.value, fontSize: fontSize.value })
}

function saveSettings() {
  const settings = { theme: theme.value, fontSize: fontSize.value }
  localStorage.setItem(STORAGE_KEY, JSON.stringify(settings))
  emit('settings-changed', settings)
}

function resetSettings() {
  theme.value = 'light'
  fontSize.value = 16
  localStorage.removeItem(STORAGE_KEY)
  emit('settings-changed', { theme: theme.value, fontSize: fontSize.value })
}

onMounted(() => {
  loadSettings()
})
</script>

THEORY.title: Appendix A: Pinia and Router Guards (Optional)
THEORY.subtitle: Chapter overview
THEORY.html:
The Week 11 slides now cover Pinia properly (stores, state, getters, actions, the MiniShop example and navigation guards). Start with Pinia: state, getters and actions and Navigation guards. The short examples below are kept as a quick reminder of the same ideas.

// src/stores/counter.js  (setup-store style)
import { ref, computed } from 'vue'
import { defineStore } from 'pinia'
export const useCounterStore = defineStore('counter', () => {
  const count = ref(0)
  const doubled = computed(() => count.value * 2)
  function increment() { count.value++ }
  return { count, doubled, increment }       // everything you want to expose
})

<script setup>
import { useCounterStore } from '@/stores/counter'
const store = useCounterStore()              // same instance in every component
</script>
<template><button @click="store.increment()">{{ store.count }} / {{ store.doubled }}</button></template>

A router guard can redirect unauthenticated users to a login page:

router.beforeEach((to) => {
  const auth = useAuthStore()
  if (to.meta.requiresAuth && !auth.isLoggedIn) return { path: '/login', query: { redirect: to.fullPath } }
})

When to use Pinia: when two unrelated components need the same data (a cart, a logged-in user); props/emits are for parent-child only. main.js already calls app.use(createPinia()) [wk5 example main.js].

THEORY.title: Verification vs validation
THEORY.subtitle: Two different questions about quality
THEORY.html:
Testing asks two separate questions [Wk10a slides]. Keep the wording straight, because exams ask you to tell them apart.

VerificationValidation
Question“Are we building the product right?”“Are we building the right product?”
Checks thatthe software conforms to the specification and designthe software meets the users’ real needs
Focuscorrectnessfitness for purpose
Whenduring developmentnear or after completion

Worked example

Requirement: “Lock an account after five consecutive failed logins.”

  • Verification: review the design and code to confirm the threshold is exactly 5 and the lockout works as specified.
  • Validation: the code is correct, but users on phones mistype passwords and get locked out too often. After feedback the team allows 10 attempts or adds a CAPTCHA. The product now meets the users’ actual need.

Memory hook: verify = spec (did we follow it?), validate = user (is it what they wanted?). Good testing needs both.

THEORY.title: Regression testing and test-driven development (TDD)
THEORY.subtitle: Re-test after changes; write the test first
THEORY.html:
Regression testing

Regression testing re-runs previously passed test cases after the software is changed, to confirm existing features still work [Wk10a slides]. A small change in one place can break another, and regression tests catch these side effects.

RetestingRegression testing
Verifiesthat one specific bug is now fixedthat existing features still work after a change
Usestest cases tied to that bugtests of the changed and the unaffected functionality

Teams automate regression tests (JUnit and pytest for code; Selenium, Cypress and Playwright for web apps) and run them in a CI/CD pipeline whenever new code is committed.

Test-driven development

TDD means writing the test before the code. It applies to unit testing and follows the Red-Green-Refactor cycle:

StepWhat you do
RedWrite a test for the behaviour you want. It should fail, because the code does not exist yet.
GreenWrite the simplest code that makes the test pass. It need not be perfect.
RefactorImprove structure, readability and performance while the tests keep passing.

THEORY.title: Load testing
THEORY.subtitle: Normal expected traffic, not extreme
THEORY.html:
Load testing is a kind of performance testing. It checks that a system meets its performance requirements under its anticipated workload [Wk10a slides].

  • The emphasis is expected, normal usage. Extreme conditions beyond that are a stress test.
  • Example: a shop expected to support 1000 concurrent users. A load test checks it handles 1000 users with acceptable response times.
  • A load-testing tool simulates many virtual users (processes or threads that behave like real users) running realistic scenarios.
  • Tools for web apps: Apache JMeter, k6 (scripts written in JavaScript), LoadRunner.

Do not mix these up: load test = expected traffic; stress test = beyond expected limits.

THEORY.title: Unit vs integration vs E2E tests
THEORY.subtitle: Scope: how much is involved
THEORY.html:
The three test types differ in what they test, their scope and how many components are involved [Wk10a, 10b and 10c slides].

Test typeWhat is testedComponents involvedGoalTool in this course
Unita single unit: a function, method, class (in Vue, a component)one component in isolationan individual unit works correctlyVitest
Integrationthe interaction between units or modulestwo or more integrated componentsthe components work correctly togetherVitest + Vue Test Utils
End-to-end (E2E)the complete system from the user’s perspectivethe whole app: UI, APIs, databasescomplete user workflows function correctlyPlaywright

Ask yourself: Vitest asks “does this piece of code work?” Playwright asks “can the user complete a task?”

In a Vue app, a component counts as a unit, so a component test is a kind of unit test. Details: Component tests, Integration tests, E2E tests.

THEORY.title: Anatomy of a unit test: describe, it, expect
THEORY.subtitle: Suite, test case, assertion, matcher
THEORY.html:
Vitest is a modern unit and integration testing framework optimised for Vite projects such as Vue 3 apps [Wk10a slides]. A unit test of a function calls it and compares the actual result with the expected one.

// function under test (SimpleFunction.js)
export function add(a, b) { return a + b }

// test file (SimpleFunction.spec.js)
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest'
import { add } from './SimpleFunction'

describe('TestSuite1: add', () => {                 // a suite: a group of related tests
  it('Test1: adds two positive numbers', () => {    // one test case
    expect(add(2, 3)).toBe(5)                       // an assertion
    expect(add(1, 3)).toBe(4)
    expect(add(999, 999)).toBe(1998)
  })
})
PieceMeaning
describe(name, fn)defines a test suite, a group of related test cases
it(name, fn) / test(name, fn)defines one test case. They are identical; pick one and stay consistent in a file
expect(actual)creates an expectation: the actual result you want to check
.toBe(expected)a matcher: the actual value must equal the expected value exactly
expect(...).toBe(...)together an assertion. If actual equals expected the test passes, otherwise it fails

Plain English for the example: “In the test suite for add, verify that 2 + 3 gives 5, 1 + 3 gives 4 and 999 + 999 gives 1998.”

THEORY.title: Running Vitest
THEORY.subtitle: Install, run one file, watch mode
THEORY.html:
Setup and commands from Exercise 1 [Wk10a slides, instructions_basic_unit_test.txt]:

CommandWhat it does
pnpm add -D vitestinstalls Vitest. -D means development dependency
pnpm vitest SimpleFunction.spec.jsruns only that spec file, in watch mode: saving the file re-runs the tests automatically. Press q to quit
pnpm vitestwith no file, runs every *.spec.js and *.test.js file in the folder
pnpm exec vitest run src/components/__tests__/StudentGrade.spec.jsruns once (no watch) a named spec inside a Vue project. Without a file name it runs all specs in __tests__

Put the function file and its spec in the same folder, and name the spec after the file (SimpleFunction.js and SimpleFunction.spec.js). The code is in the Week 10 code archive.

Both import { add } from "./SimpleFunction" and the file name must match in case on case-sensitive systems. The archive spec imports ./simplefunction in lowercase while the file is SimpleFunction.js; this works on Windows, so type the exact file name to be safe.

THEORY.title: Matchers: toBe, toEqual and the rest
THEORY.subtitle: Pick the matcher that fits the data
THEORY.html:
MatcherWhat it checksExample
toBe(x)exactly equal for primitives (uses Object.is). For objects it asks “same object in memory?”expect(add(2,3)).toBe(5)
toEqual(x)deep equality of objects and arrays: same contents, not same identityexpect(makeStudent("Alice",101)).toEqual({ name:"Alice", id:101, courses:[] })
toBeTruthy() / toBeFalsy()whether the value is truthy or falsy in a boolean contextexpect(isValidUsername("jacky")).toBeTruthy()
toHaveLength(n)the .length of an array or stringexpect([1,2,3]).toHaveLength(3)
toContain(x)an array contains an item, or a string contains a substringexpect(modules).toContain("IS216")
toThrow(msg)a function throws. Wrap the call in an arrow functionexpect(() => divide(10,0)).toThrow("Division by zero")
toBeGreaterThan(n)a number is greater than nexpect(square(5)).toBeGreaterThan(20)
toMatch(regex)a string matches a patternexpect(email).toMatch(/@example\.com$/)
toHaveProperty(key)an object has that propertyexpect(user).toHaveProperty("age")
.notflips any matcherexpect(add(2,2)).not.toBe(5)

toBe vs toEqual

function makeStudent(name, id) { return { name: name, id: id, courses: [] } }

// FAILS: two different objects are never === equal
// expect(makeStudent('Alice', 101)).toBe({ name: 'Alice', id: 101, courses: [] })

// PASSES: toEqual compares the contents recursively
expect(makeStudent('Alice', 101)).toEqual({ name: 'Alice', id: 101, courses: [] })

Rule of thumb: primitives use toBe(); objects and arrays use toEqual(). toBe() is one cheap value comparison; toEqual() runs a recursive deep-equality check, which is wasted effort on a simple number or string.

JavaScript's falsy values are false, 0, '', null, undefined and NaN. toBeTruthy() passes for 1, 'yes' and even []. The matcher examples [Wk10a slides, MoreFunctions.spec.js] are in the code archive.

THEORY.title: Choosing good test cases
THEORY.subtitle: Cover categories of input, then edges
THEORY.html:
Three tests for add cover three categories of input [Wk10a slides]: positive + positive, negative + positive, negative + negative. That is good input coverage, but the suite can be better with edge cases:

expect(add(0, 0)).toBe(0)             // both zero
expect(add(0, 5)).toBe(5)             // zero and positive
expect(add(5, 0)).toBe(5)             // positive and zero
expect(add(1000000, 1)).toBe(1000001) // large numbers
  • Group inputs into categories (typical, boundary, invalid) and test at least one of each.
  • Boundaries matter most: for a grade rule “A from 80”, test 79 and 80 (the StudentGrade slides list 80, 79, 70, 69, 60, 59 as untested boundaries).
  • Invalid input (negative numbers, undefined, strings) is another category that is often forgotten.

THEORY.title: Component tests in Vue
THEORY.subtitle: Mount one component in isolation
THEORY.html:
In a Vue app a component is a “unit”, so a component test is unit testing, usually done by the developer who wrote the component [Wk10b slides]. You mount the component with Vue Test Utils, pass props, interact with it and assert on what it renders.

import { mount } from '@vue/test-utils'
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest'
import StudentGrade from '../StudentGrade.vue'

describe('StudentGrade', () => {
  it('displays grade A when score is 85', () => {
    const wrapper = mount(StudentGrade, { props: { score: 85 } })   // props sent straight in
    expect(wrapper.text()).toContain('Grade: A')                    // rendered text
  })
  it('uses red text for failing grades', () => {
    const wrapper = mount(StudentGrade, { props: { score: 45 } })
    expect(wrapper.attributes('style')).toContain('red')            // computed colour
  })
})

Worked example: StudentGrade

The component receives score as a prop, computes the letter grade (A from 80, B from 70, C from 60, otherwise F) and shows it in green for A, B, C and red for F. The test sends the score directly; StudentProfile is never used.

TestInputExpectedPurpose
(1) grade A85Grade: AA range
(2) grade B75Grade: BB range
(3) grade C65Grade: CC range
(4) grade F45Grade: Ffailing grade
(5) green for passing85style contains greencomputed colour
(6) red for failing (you write it)45style contains redcomputed colour

It tests two things: the business logic (the computed property turns a score into a grade) and the presentation (the HTML shows the grade and the colour). Not tested here but worth adding: boundary values and invalid input.

Useful Vue Test Utils calls

CallUse
mount(Component, { props })render the real component with props
wrapper.text()all visible text
wrapper.attributes("style")an attribute value, such as the inline style
wrapper.findAll("button")find elements (then [i] to pick one)
await el.trigger("click")simulate a user event; await it so the DOM updates before you assert
wrapper.emitted("event-name")events the component emitted, as an array of argument arrays

Code: Ex2 Student components and Ex2a CourseReview and RatingSelector in the code archive.

THEORY.title: Stubs: testing a parent without its children
THEORY.subtitle: Replace children with lightweight fakes
THEORY.html:
When the component under test contains child components, a stub replaces a child with a lightweight “fake” so only the parent’s own job is tested [Wk10b slides (optional)]. StudentProfile only passes props to StudentName and StudentGrade, so the test checks exactly that.

it('passes the correct name to StudentName', () => {
  const wrapper = mount(StudentProfile, {
    props: { name: 'Alice', score: 85 },
    global: {
      stubs: {
        StudentName: {                              // custom stub: echoes the prop it receives
          props: ['name'],
          template: '<div>Name: {{ name }}</div>'
        },
        StudentGrade: true                          // automatic stub: an empty placeholder
      }
    }
  })
  expect(wrapper.text()).toContain('Name: Alice')
})
Kind of stubSyntaxUse when
Custom stuban object with props and a templateyou need to see the props the child received
Automatic stubChildName: trueyou do not need the child at all in this test

StudentProfile has five tests: four check that name and score reach the right child (including a different name and a different score), and the fifth stubs both children and checks that both render with the right props at the same time.

THEORY.title: What to test: fragile vs robust tests
THEORY.subtitle: Test behaviour, not implementation
THEORY.html:
A component test should check the component’s behaviour and contract, not everything [Wk10b slides]. Ask: “If this feature breaks, would a user or another developer care?”

Usually worth testingUsually not worth testing
props: does it render correctly when props change?every HTML tag
conditional rendering and different statesevery CSS class
user interactions: clicks, typing, selectionsthe exact HTML structure
emitted eventsframework functionality (Vue already tests itself)
computed values and important business logic
important links and buttons: correct URLs and actions

Fragile vs robust

Fragile testRobust test
Fails whenharmless refactoring happens, even though the software still worksonly when the observable behaviour changes unexpectedly
Depends onimplementation details (a function name, a button ID)what the user sees and can do
Effectneeds frequent updates; discourages refactoringsurvives internal refactoring

Example: a login test that asserts authenticateUser was called breaks the moment a developer removes that function, even if login still works. It also breaks when the button’s ID is renamed. A robust test instead checks the outcome: can the user log in?

Rule of thumb: “Test behaviour, not implementation.”

THEORY.title: Integration tests
THEORY.subtitle: Mount the real components together
THEORY.html:
When two or more components interacting with each other are tested together, it is an integration test [Wk10b slides]. Unlike the component tests there are no stubs: the real StudentProfile, StudentName and StudentGrade are mounted and exercised as a group.

it('displays grade A for score 85', () => {
  const wrapper = mount(StudentProfile, { props: { name: 'Alice', score: 85 } })
  expect(wrapper.text()).toContain('Alice')        // StudentName received and showed the name
  expect(wrapper.text()).toContain('Grade: A')     // StudentGrade computed and showed the grade
})
TestInputExpected
(1) grade AAlice, 85Alice and Grade: A
(2) grade BBob, 75Bob and Grade: B
(3) grade CCharlie, 65Charlie and Grade: C
(4) grade F (you write it)David, 45David and Grade: F

These tests verify props are passed correctly, the name is displayed and the grade is computed. They deliberately do not check the text colour: that is already covered by StudentGrade’s own component tests, so the integration test focuses on collaboration, not CSS details.

Component testIntegration test
Scopeone component, children stubbedseveral real components together
Questiondoes this component do its own job?do these components work correctly together?
Failure points toa bug inside that componenta bug in how components communicate

THEORY.title: Testing emitted events (Ex2a: CourseReview and RatingSelector)
THEORY.subtitle: The child emits, the parent listens
THEORY.html:
Exercise 2a (homework) uses a different communication path [Wk10b slides]: the child emits a custom event and the parent listens, instead of the parent passing props down.

ComponentResponsibilities
CourseReview (parent)keeps rating in state; receives rating-selected from the child; updateRating() updates it; shows “Your rating: n” and feedback (“Thank you for your positive feedback!” for 4 or above, otherwise “We will work to improve the course.”)
RatingSelector (child)five buttons (1-5); keeps its own selected rating; selectRating() emits rating-selected; shows “Excellent!” (4-5), “Good” (2-3) or “Poor” (1)

Component test: RatingSelector

const wrapper = mount(RatingSelector)
expect(wrapper.findAll('button')).toHaveLength(5)               // five buttons

await wrapper.findAll('button')[0].trigger('click')             // click rating 1
expect(wrapper.text()).toContain('Poor')

await wrapper.findAll('button')[3].trigger('click')             // click rating 4
expect(wrapper.emitted('rating-selected')).toBeTruthy()         // the event was emitted...
expect(wrapper.emitted('rating-selected')[0]).toEqual([4])      // ...with payload 4 (an array of args)

Component test: CourseReview with a stub child

const RatingSelectorStub = { template: '<div></div>', emits: ['rating-selected'] }

it('displays the initial rating of 0', () => {
  expect(mount(CourseReview).text()).toContain('Your rating: 0')
})
it('updates when the child emits rating-selected', async () => {
  const wrapper = mount(CourseReview, { global: { stubs: { RatingSelector: RatingSelectorStub } } })
  wrapper.findComponent(RatingSelectorStub).vm.$emit('rating-selected', 5)   // the "child" emits
  await wrapper.vm.$nextTick()                                               // let the DOM update
  expect(wrapper.text()).toContain('Your rating: 5')
  expect(wrapper.text()).toContain('Thank you for your positive feedback!')
})

The last test is a contract test: it talks to the parent the way the real child would (by emitting), rather than reaching inside and calling its methods. Tests 2 and 3 in the archive call wrapper.vm.updateRating() directly, which depends on the implementation and is more fragile.

Integration test

Mount CourseReview without stubs and click the real buttons: click 5 gives “Your rating: 5” and the positive message; click 4 the same; clicks on 3, 2 and 1 give the improvement message. It verifies the whole chain: user click → child emits event → parent updates state → DOM shows the result.

Full files: Ex2a in the code archive.

THEORY.title: End-to-end testing and the tool landscape
THEORY.subtitle: The whole app from the user’s view
THEORY.html:
End-to-end (E2E) testing verifies that the entire application works from the user’s perspective by testing complete workflows across the frontend, backend, database and APIs, in a production-like environment [Wk10c slides]. It tests complete user workflows, simulates real user interactions and runs against the app as a whole.

ToolPrimary useBrowsersAutomatic waitingLanguagesBest for
PlaywrightE2E testingChrome, Edge, Firefox, SafariYesJS, TypeScript, Python, Java, .NETmodern web apps
Puppeteerbrowser automationmainly Chrome/EdgeNoJS, TypeScriptscraping, PDFs, screenshots
CypressE2E testingChrome, Edge, FirefoxYesJS, TypeScriptfrontend E2E, beginners
SeleniumE2E testingalmost all browsersNoJava, Python, C#, JS and moreenterprise and legacy apps

Automatic waiting (Playwright and Cypress) means the tool waits for an element or page update to be ready before acting or asserting. This makes tests more reliable and removes arbitrary delays. Without it, a test can fail because it acted too early even though the app works.

Only Playwright is covered in this course. Playwright is an open-source framework from Microsoft that drives Chromium (Edge, Chrome), Firefox and WebKit (Safari).

THEORY.title: Playwright workflow: install, record, run
THEORY.subtitle: Ex3: a login page
THEORY.html:
A Playwright test follows five steps: launch a browser, navigate to the app, interact with the page, verify the results, close the browser [Wk10c slides].

Set up

  1. Install: pnpm create playwright. Choose JavaScript, put tests in tests, no GitHub Actions workflow, install the browsers. You get tests/example.spec.js.
  2. Check it works: pnpm playwright test (6 tests pass: 2 tests × 3 browsers). Report: pnpm exec playwright show-report, then open the URL it prints (port 9323).
  3. Install the Playwright Test for VS Code extension (Microsoft). A Testing (lab-flask) icon appears; Test Explorer lists your tests and a play button runs them.
  4. Host the page under test, e.g. pnpm dlx http-server in the folder with index.html, then open http://127.0.0.1:8080. (dlx runs a package temporarily without installing it.)

Record, then edit

  1. In Test Explorer click Record new. A browser opens; a test-1.spec.ts file is generated as you act.
  2. Enter the URL, type admin / 1234, click Login, click “Welcome Admin!”, then close the browser.
  3. Clean up the recording: remove unneeded statements and replace the last click with an assertion.
  4. Rename the test (test is the default name) to something descriptive, e.g. “should successfully log in with valid credentials”.
await expect(page.getByText('Welcome Admin!')).toBeVisible()

Record a second test for a failed login (an invalid account such as Admin/abcd) and assert the text “Login Failed”. Run all tests with the play button on the tests folder. To see a failure, deliberately break one assertion and read the error, or use the Debug icon to set breakpoints and step through. Do not write failing tests on purpose in real work.

THEORY.title: Reading a recorded test
THEORY.subtitle: Locators, await, and the three stages
THEORY.html:
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('should successfully log in with valid credentials', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('http://127.0.0.1:8080/');                                   // (1) setup
  await page.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'Username' }).fill('admin');         // (2) actions
  await page.locator('#password').fill('1234');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Login' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByText('Welcome Admin!')).toBeVisible();                // (3) assert
});
PieceMeaning
test(name, fn)defines a test case (the same idea as it())
async / awaitthe function is asynchronous; await pauses until that step finishes. Without it Playwright could look for the Username box before the page has loaded
pagethe browser page controlled by Playwright
page.goto(url)navigate to a URL
page.getByRole("button", { name: "Login" })locate by role and accessible name, then act (.click(), .fill(), .press())
page.getByText(...) / page.locator("#id")locate by visible text or CSS selector
expect(locator).toBeVisible()the assertion: “I expect this text to be visible on the page”

Most tests have three stages: (1) setup (go to the page), (2) actions (enter credentials and log in), (3) assert (verify the result).

A recorded test ends with a click on the result text. A click is not a check: change it to expect(...).toBeVisible(), otherwise the test passes even when the wrong message appears. (The archive’s third test logs in with a wrong user name but asserts “Welcome Admin!”. The app correctly shows “Login Failed”, so that test fails: it exists to show you what a failing test report looks like.)

THEORY.title: Ex3a: E2E test for a Vue app
THEORY.subtitle: Fill a form, check the grade
THEORY.html:
Host the Vue app from Exercise 2 and replace Ex2.vue with the version that shows a form for name and score [Wk10c slides]. The workflow to test: enter a name and a score, click Submit, then see the name and the correct letter grade.

await page.goto('http://localhost:5173/Ex2');
await page.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'Name:' }).fill('George');
await page.getByRole('spinbutton', { name: 'Score:' }).fill('49');     // number input = spinbutton role
await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit' }).click();
await expect(page.getByText('George')).toBeVisible();
await expect(page.getByText('Grade: F')).toBeVisible();

The model solution repeats this for four students (49 gives F, 59 gives F, 60 gives C, 80 gives A), so the boundaries 59/60 and 80 are covered. Number inputs are found with the spinbutton role.

VitestPlaywright
Asksdoes this piece of code work?can the user complete a task?
Runs ina simulated DOM (jsdom)a real browser against the running app
Needs a servernoyes (the app must be running)
Levelunit, component, integrationend-to-end

Complete test files: Ex3 and Ex3a code.

THEORY.title: Composables: reusable stateful logic
THEORY.subtitle: A function built on the Composition API
THEORY.html:
A composable is a function that uses Vue’s Composition API to encapsulate and reuse stateful logic [Wk11 slides]. Think of it as a self-contained module of reactive state (ref, reactive), computed properties and methods.

Key characteristic: a plain utility function only does stateless calculations (e.g. formatting a date). A composable manages reactive data over time. The name starts with use.

// composables/useCounter.js
import { ref, computed } from 'vue'

export function useCounter(initialValue = 0) {
  // 1. Reactive State
  const count = ref(initialValue)

  // 2. Computed Properties
  const doubleCount = computed(() => count.value * 2)

  // 3. Methods / Actions
  function increment() {
    count.value++
  }

  function decrement() {
    count.value--
  }

  function reset() {
    count.value = initialValue
  }

  // 4. Return reactive state and methods
  return {
    count,
    doubleCount,
    increment,
    decrement,
    reset
  }
}

<script setup>
import { useCounter } from '../composables/useCounter'
const { count, doubleCount, increment, decrement, reset } = useCounter(10)   // destructure state and methods
</script>

Composables do NOT share state. Every call to useCounter() creates its own new count, so two components each calling it have separate counters. To share one piece of state across components, use a store (Pinia).

Full files in the code archive.

THEORY.title: Why state management: prop drilling
THEORY.subtitle: Shared data needs one source of truth
THEORY.html:
State is data that affects what the UI displays: the logged-in user and token, cart items and quantities, a products list from an API, loading and error flags [Wk11 slides]. Key idea: state changes → the UI updates automatically. Every component already manages its own state with ref.

The problem: prop drilling

In a single-page app many components need the same data. If the cart lives only in a parent component, you must pass it through props and events across many layers:

  • the Navbar needs the cart count
  • the Product card needs “add to cart”
  • the Cart page needs totals and actions

That is messy, hard to refactor and hard to share across routes (pages). This is prop drilling. A store solves it by being a central source of truth that any component can read and update.

What belongs in a store

Put in a storeKeep in the component
data used in many places (user shown in the navbar)local data such as whether an element on one page is visible
data kept across pages (a long multi-step form)
a products list reused by the list page and the detail page

Not every app needs global state. If yours does, Pinia makes it simple. If only a parent and child share data, props and emits are enough (see Components: props, slots, emits).

THEORY.title: Pinia: state, getters and actions
THEORY.subtitle: The official Vue 3 store
THEORY.html:
Pinia is the official store library for Vue 3 [Wk11 slides]. A store has three concepts, which mirror a component:

PiniaMeaningComponent equivalentSetup-store form
stateshared reactive datadataref(...)
gettersderived valuescomputedcomputed(...)
actionsmethods (sync or async) that update statemethodsplain functions

Install and register

pnpm add pinia        # only if the project does not already list pinia in package.json

import { createApp } from 'vue'
import { createPinia } from 'pinia'

import App from './App.vue'
import router from './router'

// Import Bootstrap CSS and JS
import 'bootstrap/dist/css/bootstrap.min.css'
import 'bootstrap/dist/js/bootstrap.bundle.min.js'

const app = createApp(App)

app.use(createPinia())
app.use(router)

app.mount('#app')

Define a store

Use defineStore(id, setupFunction). The first argument is a unique id across the app. Name the result use…Store by convention.

import { ref, computed } from 'vue'
import axios from 'axios'
import { defineStore } from "pinia";

export const useProductsStore = defineStore('products', () => {
  // state properties
  const products = ref([])
  const loading = ref(false)
  const error = ref(null)

  // action
  async function fetchProducts() {
    loading.value = true
    error.value = null

    try {
        const response = await axios("http://localhost:8000/products");
        products.value = await response.data;
    } catch (e) {
      error.value = "Failed to load products";
      console.error(e.message)
    } finally {
      loading.value = false;
    }
  }
  
  return { products, loading, error, fetchProducts }
})

Return everything you want to expose (return { products, loading, error, fetchProducts }). A state, getter or action left out of the returned object is not available outside the store and the app may break.

A store is created only when useXxxStore() is first called inside a component’s <script setup> (or another store).

THEORY.title: Using a store in components
THEORY.subtitle: State, getters and actions
THEORY.html:
<script setup>
import { onMounted } from "vue"
import { useProductsStore } from "@/stores/products"     // @ = the src folder (Vite alias)
import ProductCard from "../components/ProductCard.vue"

const productsStore = useProductsStore()
onMounted(() => {
  if (productsStore.products.length === 0) productsStore.fetchProducts()   // action: only fetch once
})
</script>

<template>
  <ProductCard v-for="p in productsStore.products" :key="p.id" :product="p" />   <!-- state in the template -->
</template>
PartHow to use itExample
Stateread and write it directly on the store instance, in script or template, and bind it with v-model/v-bindcart.items, <input v-model="store.count">, store.count++
Gettersused like a computed: no parenthesescart.totalPrice.toFixed(2)
Actionscalled like methods, from script or a template eventstore.randomizeCounter(), @click="cart.addToCart(product)"

Getters and actions in the cart store

const items = ref([])                                          // state
const itemCount  = computed(() => items.value.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.qty, 0))             // getter
const totalPrice = computed(() => items.value.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price * i.qty, 0))   // getter
const isEmpty    = computed(() => items.value.length === 0)                                    // getter

function removeFromCart(productId) {                           // action
  items.value = items.value.filter((i) => i.productId !== productId)
}

Actions hold business logic, for example “give a discount when the order is over $50”. Stores are reactive like ref(): when the cart store changes, every component reading it (navbar badge, cart page) updates.

Inside a setup store, state is ref so you write items.value; outside the store you read store.items with no .value (Pinia unwraps it).

THEORY.title: MiniShop: the running example
THEORY.subtitle: Products, cart and login across pages
THEORY.html:
The Week 11 running example is MiniShop, an e-commerce-style app where several pages need the same shared state [Wk11 slides]. Users can browse products, add to cart, change quantities, see the cart count in the navbar on every page and “log in” to check out.

PartNameRole
Views (routes)ProductsView (/products)lists products, “Add to cart” buttons
CartView (/cart)items, quantities, total, Checkout
LoginView (/login)fake login to demonstrate the auth store and route guards
ComponentsNavBarcart count and login status
ProductCarda product and an add button
CartItemRowquantity controls per item
StoresuseProductsStorestate products, loading, error; action fetchProducts() (async call to the Express API)
useCartStorestate items ({productId, title, price, qty}); getters itemCount, totalPrice, isEmpty; actions addToCart, removeFromCart, increaseQty, decreaseQty, clearCart
useAuthStorestate user (null or {name, token}), loading, error; getter isLoggedIn; actions login(username, password), logout()

Data flow

  1. User clicks “Add to cart” → calls cartStore.addToCart(product).
  2. The store updates items[].
  3. The navbar reads cartStore.itemCount.
  4. The cart page reads cartStore.items and cartStore.totalPrice.

Run it

PartCommands
Frontend (MiniShop)cd example, pnpm install, pnpm dev
Backend (Node + Express mock API, from server.zip)cd server/products, pnpm install, pnpm dev. Serves GET /products, POST /login (accepts any username/password), POST /checkout

Product data is queried from the backend, so start both. The API also has POST /orders and GET /orders for Exercise 4, protected by Authorization: Bearer fake-token-123. The final demo: / redirects to /products; adding items updates “Cart (3)” in the navbar; clicking Cart while logged out redirects to /login because of the navigation guard. Code: server, stores, views and components.

THEORY.title: Persisting store state with localStorage
THEORY.subtitle: Survive a page refresh (Ex1 and Ex3)
THEORY.html:
A store lives in memory, so a refresh resets it. To keep the cart and the login, save to localStorage [Wk11 slides, Exercises 1 and 3]. See Saving data in the browser.

ExerciseDo this
Ex1 Part Aon store creation, initialise items from localStorage (an empty array if nothing is stored)
Ex1 Part Bsave to localStorage every time the cart changes (add, remove, increase, decrease, clear)
Ex3 Part Asave { token, username } when login succeeds; restore both when the store is created, so isLoggedIn becomes true automatically
Ex3 Part Blogout() also removes the localStorage key
Ex3 Part Cin LoginView, if already logged in, redirect to /products straight away
const STORAGE_KEY = "minishop_cart"

function loadCart() {
  try {
    const raw = localStorage.getItem(STORAGE_KEY)
    const parsed = raw ? JSON.parse(raw) : []
    return Array.isArray(parsed) ? parsed : []        // never trust stored data
  } catch { return [] }                               // corrupted JSON must not crash the app
}
function saveCart(items) { localStorage.setItem(STORAGE_KEY, JSON.stringify(items)) }

const items = ref(loadCart())                         // initial state comes from storage

localStorage stores strings: use JSON.stringify to save and JSON.parse to read, and wrap the parse in try/catch. Do not store passwords. The token is stored here only because this is a fake teaching login.

THEORY.title: Route parameters and useRoute
THEORY.subtitle: One component, many URLs
THEORY.html:
Revisiting routing from Week 4 [Wk11 slides]: App.vue contains <RouterView />, which shows the component mapped by router/index.js. Use <RouterLink to="/products"> to link. See Vue Router.

A route parameter is a changing part of the path:

{ path: "/products/:id", component: ProductDetailView }

// visiting /products/1 launches ProductDetailView with id = 1
import { useRoute } from 'vue-router'
const route = useRoute()                    // 1. initialise the route hook
const productId = route.params.id           // 2. read the parameter

Route params are always strings. route.params.id is "1", not 1, so compare with Number(route.params.id) (as the solution does with find((p) => p.id === productId.value)), otherwise 1 === "1" is false and the product is “not found”.

THEORY.title: Redirects and programmatic navigation
THEORY.subtitle: Declared in the route table, or in code
THEORY.html:
WayCodeUse
Redirect in the route table{ path: "/", redirect: "/products" }visiting / goes to /products: a default landing page, or a login page after registration
Programmatic navigationrouter.push("/products")navigate from code, e.g. after logout or login
import { useRouter } from "vue-router"
const router = useRouter()

function logout() {
  auth.logout()
  router.push("/products")        // after logout, go back to /products
}

router.push(url) changes the browser address and loads the component mapped to that route [Wk11 slides]. useRoute() (read the current route) and useRouter() (navigate) are different hooks: route = where I am; router = go somewhere.

THEORY.title: Navigation guards
THEORY.subtitle: Control who can open which route
THEORY.html:
A navigation guard is code that runs before or during navigation and decides whether a route should proceed, be blocked, or redirect to a different route [Wk11 slides]. In a single-page app it is the main tool for rules such as “only logged-in users can open /cart”, “only admins can open /admin” or “confirm before leaving a form with unsaved changes”.

// router/index.js
{ path: "/cart", component: CartView, meta: { requiresAuth: true } }     // custom metadata on the route

router.beforeEach((to) => {                    // runs before EVERY navigation
  if (!to.meta.requiresAuth) return true       // public route: allow
  const auth = useAuthStore()
  if (auth.isLoggedIn) return true             // logged in: allow
  return { path: "/login", query: { redirect: to.fullPath } }   // else: redirect to login, remembering the target
})
to propertyContainsExample
to.paththe destination path/cart
to.paramsroute parametersthe :id value
to.fullPathpath plus query string/cart?sort=asc
to.metacustom metadata from the route definition{ requiresAuth: true }
GuardRunsTypical use
router.beforeEach()before every navigation (most used)authentication, permissions
router.afterEach()after navigationanalytics, logging

Best practices

  • Use meta flags (requiresAuth, role) so one guard protects many routes.
  • Keep the guard small and delegate to a store (auth.isLoggedIn, auth.hasRole(...)).
  • Use the redirect-back-after-login pattern: send the user to /login?redirect=/cart; after login, router.push(route.query.redirect || "/products").

Guards are not real security. They run in the browser, which the client (possibly malicious) fully controls, so they only improve navigation control and user experience. Your Express API must still verify tokens, credentials and permissions on the server.

Guards improve security (client-side UI control), user experience (redirect to login, prevent data loss) and correctness (required data exists before a page renders).

THEORY.subtitle: Detail page, persistence, orders

The rest of the action (loading.value = false in finally) already does this, so rewrite the first two lines to match.

THEORY.title: Week 11 recap
THEORY.subtitle: Take-away messages
THEORY.html:
• State management solves shared-data problems in single-page apps: when several components or pages need the same data (cart count, user session, product list), a store avoids prop drilling.
  • Pinia structures app-level logic: state for shared reactive data, getters for derived values (total price), actions for business logic and async API calls.
  • Stores and routing work together: views fetch data in onMounted(), reuse cached store data across routes, and the UI updates everywhere when store state changes.
  • Route guards use store state: put meta flags such as requiresAuth on routes, check them in router.beforeEach(), and use the redirect-back-after-login pattern.
  • Good UX handles loading and error states, persists key state (cart, auth) with localStorage when needed, and remembers that guards are for UX only: the backend must still enforce authentication and authorisation.
NeedUse
reuse stateful logic, separate state per usea composable (useXxx())
share one state across components and pagesa Pinia store
parent to child, one levelprops (and emits back up)
show a different component per URLVue Router
block or redirect a routea navigation guard with meta

THEORY.title: Playwright in VS Code: Test Explorer, run, debug
THEORY.subtitle: The extension workflow
THEORY.html:
The Playwright Test for VS Code extension (published by Microsoft) lets you run, record and debug tests without typing commands [Wk10c slides, Ex3 setup].

  1. Open Extensions (Ctrl+Shift+X), search for “Playwright Test for VS Code” and install it. Restart VS Code if needed.
  2. A Testing icon (a laboratory flask) appears on the Activity Bar. It opens Test Explorer. If it says “No tests have been found in this workspace yet”, open the folder where you installed Playwright.
  3. Expand tests to see example.spec.js. Right-click it and choose Go To Test to open the source.
  4. Click the play icon beside a file, a single test or the tests folder to run it. Results appear in the Test Results tab of the Panel (View → Appearance → Panel if it is hidden).
  5. Use the Debug icon instead of play to set breakpoints, step over a failure and inspect variables.
  6. Use Record new to open a browser (with a pink page background) and generate a spec file as you click.
TaskWhere
run all testsplay icon on the tests folder, or pnpm playwright test
run one test or fileplay icon beside it
see why a test failedTest Results tab, or the HTML report (pnpm exec playwright show-report)
step through a failing testDebug icon

The tests themselves are explained in Reading a recorded test.

THEORY.title: Role-based authorisation: an admin-only route
THEORY.subtitle: Authentication vs authorisation
THEORY.html:
Authentication asks “who are you?” (logged in or not). Authorisation asks “what may you do?” (your role). The extended Week 11 exercise guide adds a role to the login and an /admin route that only an admin may open [Wk11 exercise guide (temp.js), Exercise 4].

  1. Backend: the login response includes a role, e.g. username === "admin" ? "admin" : "user".
  2. Store: keep user.role and add a getter isAdmin = computed(() => user.value?.role === "admin"). Persist the role with the rest of the login.
  3. Route: add meta: { requiresAuth: true, requiresRole: "admin" } to /admin.
  4. Guard: first check login, then check the role.
router.beforeEach((to) => {
  const auth = useAuthStore()

  // 1) authentication
  if (to.meta.requiresAuth && !auth.isLoggedIn) {
    return { path: "/login", query: { redirect: to.fullPath } }
  }

  // 2) authorisation (role)
  if (to.meta.requiresRole && auth.user?.role !== to.meta.requiresRole) {
    return { path: "/products" }          // wrong role: send them somewhere safe
  }
  return true
})

Test flow: log in as student, who can open /cart but not /admin; log in as admin, who can open /admin too. The archive version shows an alert("Access denied: admin only"); a toast component is nicer in a real app.

This is UI control only. Hiding /admin in the browser does not protect admin data: the Express API must check the token and the role on every admin request. See Navigation guards.

Files: extended exercise guide in the code archive.

<!-- StudentGrade.vue 
StudentGrade component is the child component of StudentProfile.

                ↓
    calculates letter grade
                ↓
    render the letter grade in red (fail)or green (pass)
-->

<script setup>
import { computed } from 'vue'

const props = defineProps({
    score: Number
})

const letterGrade = computed(() => {
    if (props.score >= 80) return 'A'
    if (props.score >= 70) return 'B'
    if (props.score >= 60) return 'C'
    return 'F'
})

const gradeColor = computed(() => {
    return letterGrade.value === 'F'
        ? 'red'
        : 'green'
})
</script>

<template>
    <div :style="{ color: gradeColor }">
        Grade: {{ letterGrade }}
    </div>
</template>

/*
Component Test for CourseReview.vue

Since RatingSelector is assumed to be tested separately, CourseReview should focus on:
✓ initial rating displayed
✓ responds correctly when a rating-selected event is received
✓ displays positive feedback for high ratings
✓ displays improvement feedback for low ratings
✓ updates the displayed rating value

Notice that none of these tests care:
✗ how many buttons RatingSelector has
✗ what messages RatingSelector shows
✗ how RatingSelector generates ratings
Those belong to RatingSelector's test suite

This separation is exactly what makes component testing useful: each component is tested against its public contract, and integration tests can then verify that the components work together.

There are 4 tests below: 
    Test1: Initial state
    Test2: High rating path
    Test3: Low rating path
    Test4: Child component emits event → parent updates

Tests 2 & 3 are testing the internal implementation of CourseReview
Test 4 is testing the component contract between CourseReview and RatingSelector:
    emits rating-selected
            ↓
    CourseReview updates
This test interacts with the component the way another component would, rather than reaching inside and calling its methods.
*/

import { mount } from '@vue/test-utils'
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest'
import CourseReview from '@/components/CourseReview.vue'

const RatingSelectorStub = {
    template: '<div></div>',
    emits: ['rating-selected']
}

describe('CourseReview', () => {
    // Verify that the initial rating displayed is 0.
    it('displays the initial rating of 0', () => {
        const wrapper = mount(CourseReview)

        expect(wrapper.text()).toContain('Your rating: 0')
    })

    // Verify that a high rating displays a positive feedback message.
    it('displays positive feedback when the rating is 4', async () => {
        const wrapper = mount(CourseReview)
        wrapper.vm.updateRating(4)
        await wrapper.vm.$nextTick()

        expect(wrapper.text()).toContain('Thank you for your positive feedback!')
    })

    // Verify that a low rating displays an improvement message.
    it('displays improvement feedback when the rating is 2', async () => {
        const wrapper = mount(CourseReview)
        wrapper.vm.updateRating(2)
        await wrapper.vm.$nextTick()

        expect(wrapper.text()).toContain('We will work to improve the course.')
    })

    // Verify that the parent updates its displayed rating when the child component emits a rating-selected event.
    it('updates the rating when RatingSelector emits rating-selected', async () => {
        const wrapper = mount(CourseReview, {
            global: {
                stubs: {
                    RatingSelector: RatingSelectorStub
                }
            }
        })

        const ratingSelector = wrapper.findComponent(RatingSelectorStub)

        ratingSelector.vm.$emit('rating-selected', 5)
        await wrapper.vm.$nextTick()

        expect(wrapper.text()).toContain('Your rating: 5')
        expect(wrapper.text()).toContain('Thank you for your positive feedback!')
    })

})

// composables/useCounter.js
import { ref, computed } from 'vue'

export function useCounter(initialValue = 0) {
  // 1. Reactive State
  const count = ref(initialValue)

  // 2. Computed Properties
  const doubleCount = computed(() => count.value * 2)

  // 3. Methods / Actions
  function increment() {
    count.value++
  }

  function decrement() {
    count.value--
  }

  function reset() {
    count.value = initialValue
  }

  // 4. Return reactive state and methods
  return {
    count,
    doubleCount,
    increment,
    decrement,
    reset
  }
}

import { ref, computed } from 'vue'
import axios from 'axios'
import { defineStore } from "pinia";

export const useProductsStore = defineStore('products', () => {
  // state properties
  const products = ref([])
  const loading = ref(false)
  const error = ref(null)

  // action
  async function fetchProducts() {
    loading.value = true
    error.value = null

    try {
        const response = await axios("http://localhost:8000/products");
        products.value = await response.data;
    } catch (e) {
      error.value = "Failed to load products";

  }

})

import { ref, computed } from 'vue'
import { defineStore } from 'pinia'

export const useCartStore = defineStore('cart', () => {
  // states
  const items = ref([]) // { productId, title, price, qty }

  // getters
  const itemCount = computed(() => items.value.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.qty, 0))

  const totalPrice = computed(() => items.value.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price * i.qty, 0))

  const isEmpty = computed(() => items.value.length === 0)

  // actions
  function addToCart(product) {
    const existing = items.value.find((i) => i.productId === product.id)
    if (existing) existing.qty += 1
    else {
      items.value.push({
        productId: product.id,
        title: product.title,
        price: product.price,
        qty: 1,
      })
    }
  }

  function removeFromCart(productId) {
    items.value = items.value.filter((i) => i.productId !== productId)
  }

  function increaseQty(productId) {
    const item = items.value.find((i) => i.productId === productId)
    if (item) item.qty += 1
  }

  function decreaseQty(productId) {
    const item = items.value.find((i) => i.productId === productId)
    if (!item) 
      return
    item.qty -= 1
    if (item.qty <= 0) {
      // remove from cart when the quantity <= 0
      removeFromCart(productId) 
      // items.value = items.value.filter((i) => i.productId !== productId)
    }
      
  }

  function clearCart() {
    items.value = []
  }

  return {items, itemCount, totalPrice, isEmpty, addToCart, removeFromCart, increaseQty, decreaseQty, clearCart}
})

auth store: login, logout, isLoggedInsrc/stores/auth.js

import { ref, computed } from 'vue'
import axios from 'axios'
import { defineStore } from 'pinia'

export const useAuthStore = defineStore('auth', () => {
  // states
  const user = ref(null) // { username }
  const token = ref(null) // "fake-token"
  const loading = ref(false)
  const error = ref(null)

  // getters
  const isLoggedIn = computed(() => !!token.value)
  // !! convert token.value into a strict boolean, keeping the original token.value result

  // actions
  async function login(username, password) {
    loading.value = true
    error.value = null

    try {
      const userInput = { username, password }
      const response = await axios.post('http://localhost:8000/login', userInput)

      const data = response.data // { token, username }

      token.value = data.token
      user.value = { username: data.username }
    } catch (e) {
      error.value = 'Login failed'
    } finally {
      loading.value = false
    }
  }

  function logout() {
    token.value = null
    user.value = null
  }

  return { user, token, loading, error, isLoggedIn, login, logout }
})

import { createRouter, createWebHistory } from 'vue-router'

import ProductsView from "../views/ProductsView.vue"
import CartView from "../views/CartView.vue"
import LoginView from "../views/LoginView.vue"

import { useAuthStore } from "../stores/auth"

const router = createRouter({
  history: createWebHistory(),
  routes: [
    { path: "/", redirect: "/products" },
    { path: "/products", component: ProductsView },
    { path: "/login", component: LoginView },
    { path: "/cart", component: CartView, meta: { requiresAuth: true } }
  ]
})

// Navigation guard (auth)
router.beforeEach((to) => {
  if (!to.meta.requiresAuth) return true

  const auth = useAuthStore();
  if (auth.isLoggedIn) return true

  return { path: "/login", query: { redirect: to.fullPath } }
})

import { ref, computed } from 'vue'
import { defineStore } from 'pinia'

// Exercise 1: Add/Modify Code below
const STORAGE_KEY = "minishop_cart"

function loadCart() {
  // Exercise 1 - Part A: Add Code Here
  try {
    const raw = localStorage.getItem(STORAGE_KEY);
    const parsed = raw ? JSON.parse(raw) : [];
    return Array.isArray(parsed) ? parsed : [];
  } catch {
    return [];
  }
}

function saveCart(items) {
  // Exercise 1 - Part B: Add Code Here
  localStorage.setItem(STORAGE_KEY, JSON.stringify(items));
}


export const useCartStore = defineStore('cart', () => {
  // states
  const items = ref(loadCart()) // { productId, title, price, qty }

  // getters
  const itemCount = computed(() => items.value.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.qty, 0))

  const totalPrice = computed(() => items.value.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price * i.qty, 0))

  const isEmpty = computed(() => items.value.length === 0)

  // actions
  function addToCart(product) {
    const existing = items.value.find((i) => i.productId === product.id)
    if (existing) existing.qty += 1
    else {
      items.value.push({
        productId: product.id,
        title: product.title,
        price: product.price,
        qty: 1,
      })
    }
    // Exercise 1 - Part B: Add Code Here
    saveCart(items.value)
  }

  function removeFromCart(productId) {
    items.value = items.value.filter((i) => i.productId !== productId)
    // Exercise 1 - Part B: Add Code Here
    saveCart(items.value)
  }

  function increaseQty(productId) {
    const item = items.value.find((i) => i.productId === productId)
    if (item) item.qty += 1
    // Exercise 1 - Part B: Add Code Here
    saveCart(items.value)
  }

  function decreaseQty(productId) {
    const item = items.value.find((i) => i.productId === productId)
    if (!item) 
      return
    item.qty -= 1
    if (item.qty <= 0) 
      items.value = items.value.filter((i) => i.productId !== productId)

    // Exercise 1 - Part B: Add Code Here
    saveCart(items.value)
  
  }

  function clearCart() {
    items.value = []
    // Exercise 1 - Part B: Add Code Here
    saveCart(items.value)
  }

  return {items, itemCount, totalPrice, isEmpty, addToCart, removeFromCart, increaseQty, decreaseQty, clearCart}
})

Ex3: auth store with localStorage and rolesrc/stores/auth.js

import { ref, computed } from 'vue'
import axios from 'axios'
import { defineStore } from 'pinia'

// Exercise 3 - Part A: Add Code Below
const STORAGE_KEY = "minishop_auth"

function loadAuth() {
  // Exercise 3 - Part A: Add Code Here
  try {
    const raw = localStorage.getItem(STORAGE_KEY)
    const parsed = raw ? JSON.parse(raw) : null

    if (!parsed || typeof parsed !== "object") 
      return { token: null, user: null }
    
    const token = typeof parsed.token === "string" ? parsed.token : null
    const username = typeof parsed.username === "string" ? parsed.username : null
    const role = typeof parsed.role === "string" ? parsed.role : null
    
    return token && username ? { token, user: { username, role } } : { token: null, user: null }
  } catch {
    return { token: null, user: null }
  }
}

function saveAuth({ token, user }) {
  // Exercise 3 - Part A: Add Code Here
  if (!token || !user?.username) return

  localStorage.setItem(
    STORAGE_KEY,
    JSON.stringify({ token, username: user.username, role: user.role || "user" })
  )
}

export const useAuthStore = defineStore('auth', () => {
  // states
  // Exercise 3 - Part A: Modify Code Below to inialize with authenicated data if any
  const loaded = loadAuth()
  const user = ref(loaded.user) // { username }
  const token = ref(loaded.token) // "fake-token"
  const loading = ref(false)
  const error = ref(null)

  // getters
  // !! convert token.value into a strict boolean, keeping the original token.value result
  const isLoggedIn = computed(() => !!token.value)

  // Exercise 5: Use computed to return true if user is an admin
  const isAdmin = computed(() => user.value?.role === "admin")
 
  // actions
  // Exercise 3 - Part A: Modify login() to persist user login 
  async function login(username, password) {
    loading.value = true
    error.value = null

    try {
      const userInput = { username, password }
      const response = await axios.post('http://localhost:8000/login', userInput)

      const data = response.data // { token, username }

      token.value = data.token
      // Exercise 5: modify code below to include user's role and save current user authentication data in localStorage
      user.value = { username: data.username, role: data.role || "user" }

      saveAuth({ token: token.value, user: user.value })
    } catch (e) {
      error.value = 'Login failed'
    } finally {
      loading.value = false
    }
  }

  // Exercise 3 - Part B: Modify logout() to remove persistence user login data
  function logout() {
    token.value = null
    user.value = null
    localStorage.removeItem(STORAGE_KEY)
  }

  function clearError() {
    error.value = null
  }

  return { user, token, loading, error, isLoggedIn, isAdmin, login, logout, clearError }
})

    { path: "/", redirect: "/products" },
    { path: "/products", component: ProductsView },
    { path: "/products/:id", component: ProductDetailView },
    { path: "/login", component: LoginView },

    { path: "/cart", component: CartView, meta: { requiresAuth: true } },

    { path: "/admin", component: AdminView, meta: { requiresAuth: true, requiresRole: "admin" } }
  ]
});

router.beforeEach((to) => {
  const auth = useAuthStore();

  // 1) Auth check
  if (to.meta.requiresAuth && !auth.isLoggedIn) {
    return { path: "/login", query: { redirect: to.fullPath } };
  }

  // 2) Role check
  if (to.meta.requiresRole) {
    const required = to.meta.requiresRole; // "admin"
    const userRole = auth.user?.role;

    if (userRole !== required) {
      // optionally show an alert; better practice is use a toast component
      alert("Access denied: admin only");
      return { path: "/products" };
    }
  }

  return true;
});

export default router;

Test flow from the guide: run the backend (node server.js) and the frontend (npm run dev); open /products and add items; /cart redirects to login when logged out; log in as student to reach the cart but not /admin; log in as admin to reach /admin; checkout creates an order and /orders lists it.

import { ref, computed } from 'vue'
import { defineStore } from 'pinia'

export const useCounterStore = defineStore('counter', () => {
  const count = ref(0)
  const doubleCount = computed(() => count.value * 2)
  function increment() {
    count.value++
  }

  return { count, doubleCount, increment }
})

Mutate arrays with push/splice or reassign with filter/map; both re-render. .sort() mutates the original, so copy first with [...arr]. Don't hardcode data or messages the grader may swap.

CHEAT.title: Axios: request cookbook
CHEAT.subtitle: Every exam Q4 follows load → add → delete → display
CHEAT.html:
import axios from 'axios'
const API_URL = 'http://localhost:8000/api'
const items = ref([]); const loading = ref(true); const error = ref('')

async function loadData() {                       // GET: on mount, re-use to refresh
  try {
    const response = await axios.get(API_URL)     // + { params: { q: 'x' } } -> ?q=x
    items.value = response.data                   // CHECK THE SHAPE: response.data.courseInfo ?
  } catch (e) { error.value = 'Failed to load' } finally { loading.value = false }
}
async function add() {                            // POST: body = 2nd argument
  try {
    const response = await axios.post(API_URL, { name: name.value, qty: Number(qty.value) })
    items.value.push(response.data.item ?? response.data)      // or await loadData()
    name.value = ''
  } catch (e) { error.value = e.response?.data?.error || e.message }
}
async function update(id) { await axios.put(`${API_URL}/${id}`, { name: name.value }); await loadData() }   // PUT/PATCH: id in URL, body 2nd
async function remove(id) {                       // DELETE: id in URL, no body (or { data: {...} } in config)
  try { await axios.delete(`${API_URL}/${id}`); items.value = items.value.filter(i => i.id !== id) }
  catch (e) { error.value = e.message }
}
onMounted(loadData)
// several at once: await Promise.all(cities.value.map(c => fetchWeather(c)))
// headers: axios.get(url, { headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` } })   POST: (url, body, { headers })
// key in .env: VITE_KEY=abc  ->  import.meta.env.VITE_KEY   (restart pnpm dev)
SituationCheck
where does the data goGET/DELETE: (url, config) POST/PUT/PATCH: (url, data, config)
responseresponse.data (payload) .status .headers
failure (non-2xx throws!)error.message error.response?.status (400, 404, 409) error.response?.data (server message) error.response undefined = server unreachable
"Failed to load" / CORS errorserver not running, wrong port/URL; look at DevTools Network
table emptywrong .data level; console.log(response.data) first
POST returns 400body keys don't match what the server expects
table not updated after writepush / filter / re-fetch the local array
show server message in UIalert(response.data.message) not a hardcoded string
StatusMeaning
200 OKGET / PUT / DELETE success
201 CreatedPOST success
400 Bad Requestmissing / invalid data
404 Not Foundid doesn't exist
409 Conflictduplicate / already taken
500 Server errorserver bug
Loading/error UI: <p v-if="loading">…</p> <p v-else-if="error">{{ error }}</p> <ul v-else>…. House style: named async function, try/catch, response/error, onMounted(loadData), no .then(). Use only Axios for HTTP.
